Climate models, whether simplified or complex, often find themselves overwhelmed by the vast number of variables involved, leading some to be irrelevant or unimportant. Dimensionality reduction methods, such as the QSS method, are utilized to pinpoint and eliminate insignificant variables, streamlining the modeling process. This reduction in variables doesn't come at the cost of substantial accuracy losses, offering improved computational efficiency and transparency. We will delve into the QSS method's inner workings and its applications within climate modeling, focusing on its utilization in identifying the most influential variables. This, in turn, enables the determination of variable interaction patterns, providing valuable insights that could be further investigated. Ultimately, our goal is to demonstrate the QSS method's utility in generating simplified, high-accuracy models from complex systems. This reduced model can then be used for policy evaluations, sensitivity analyses, and other tasks that benefit from a compact and intuitive representation of the climate system. Specifically, our work will focus on identifying the most important variables in models of carbon dioxide and nitrogen dioxide absorption. It is essential to note that while our examples come from climate modeling, the QSS method has far-reaching applications across various fields, including chemistry, biology, and economics. We encourage readers to explore these interconnected domains, highlighting the common challenges and opportunities that arise from variable interactions in dynamic models. These phenomena are not unique to climate modeling; they are ubiquitous in any context where complex systems need to be reduced to their core components. This reduction is often facilitated by non-trivial variable interactions that are hidden within the model's underlying structure. Thus, dimensionality reduction methods are of paramount importance, offering a means to extract meaningful insights from dynamic systems. These insights encompass not only variable elimination but also the identification of variable relationships and the resulting compact models that can be used for policy evaluations and sensitivity analyses. In this context, our examples are by no means exhaustive; dimensionality reduction methods are versatile tools applicable to a broad range of topics, encompassing El-Nino effects, grizzly bear migrations, epidemics, traffic flow, air pollution, utility systems, biological networks, stock market analysis, and many other domains. We look forward to seeing dimensionality reduction methods further integrate into these fields, facilitating breakthroughs in both theoretical and applied research. This collaborative exchange is already evident in the ongoing work by our research group. For instance, Dr. Schrabak is currently working with Dr. Andrew C. I. Wilson from University College London on a project that aims to utilize dimensionality reduction methods to extract and encode task-specific features into reinforcement learning

This paper presents the most comprehensive set of relativistic autoionizing state energies, wavefunctions, and energies of expansion for Au IV and Os II, along with essential data for modeling nonradiative relaxation processes in these ions. Specifically, we provide a detailed list of autoionizing state energies in the low-lying negative energy range for Au IV and Os II. Furthermore, our calculations include a set of relativistic multichannel opacities relevant to kilonova ejecta modeling, including both neutral and singly ionized Os, Ir, Pt, Au, Hg, and Tl atoms. These opacities cover a range from 1 eV to 2000 eV and are accurate to a factor of 1.5. Additionally, our work includes a set of standard (reduced) oscillator strengths for both autoionizing and non-autoionizing processes in Au IV and Os II. These oscillators strengths are accurate to an uncertainty of about 10 percent. A dedicated autoionization database for Au IV and Os II has been developed to facilitate further research and modeling efforts. Our calculated opacities and oscillator strengths are expected to contribute significantly to the understanding of kilonova spectra due to their relevance to the low-gravity, low-metallicity environment in which these events occur. Consequently, these results will also influence the development of future atomic structure software and databases. Our calculated data will be available online at the NIST Atomic Atomic Structure Center website. Moreover, a dedicated Python package, pyasf1n, has been developed to store and manage the extensive data associated with relativistic autoionizing states, facilitating easy access to the data via standard database queries. To facilitate effective treatment of obstructive symptoms associated with intestinal tumors, researchers have been advocating for a novel, automated method to segment the gastrointestinal (GI) tract in CT scans. Leveraging a massive, publicly accessible CT scan dataset with corresponding annotation files, our team developed and tested a fully automated GI canal segmentation method. This approach incorporated a modified 3D U-Net architecture, combined with a self-organizing feature map (SOM) technique to streamline data preparation, and utilized a weight average scheme for training robustness. With the capacity to handle CT scans up to 512 pixels in length, our method enables rapid deployment, demonstrating an average segmentation time of just 30 seconds. By evaluating our segmentation protocol against the original annotations, we achieved a Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) of 0.942 and a mean absolute surface distance of 0.96 mm. This high-performance outcome underscores the potential of our method to supplement clinical practices, providing an efficient, fully automated solution for clinical use. With continued advancements in deep learning, our proposed method may serve as a basic framework for more advanced clinical applications. Future studies will aim to further improve this segmentation protocol. Additionally, we calculated the predicted z-coordinate for vertebral bodies with an error of 0.96 mm and found that our results compared favorably with those of leading radiology institutions. These outstanding outcomes demonstrate the potential of our method to supplement clinical practices, providing an efficient, fully automated solution. With ongoing development, our segmentation protocol may be adapted for more complex procedures. Furthermore, we have investigated the feasibility of our method on a separate, independent dataset, revealing promising results with a DSC of 0.934 for Dice similarity coefficient and an average surface distance of 1 mm. These findings confirm the excellent generalizability of our method, highlighting the advantages of the weight average technique. To our knowledge, this study presents the first fully automated GI canal segmentation results obtained from a CT scan dataset provided by radiology institutions. These results demonstrate the potential of our method to streamline and automate clinical procedures, ultimately facilitating the detection of intestinal tumors from CT scans. Moving forward, we aim to further refine our segmentation protocol. Due to space constraints, we will provide detailed explanation and additional information in the supplementary document.

We apply this mathematical approach to handle various linear models used in compositional data analysis. Furthermore, we examine how to interpret the results of these models and perform statistical inference. The exoplanet desert around a star of a certain size (roughly 0.4-0.7 times the mass of our sun) poses a challenge in current planet formation theories, suggesting that giant planets of sub-Saturn mass are difficult to form below this boundary. However, little research has been done on the desert in lower-mass stars. Using the CORALIE/HARPS radial velocity dataset, we analyzed whether the desert exists in the mass range of 1-20 Earth masses for smaller stars, comparing the observed number of planets to those predicted by a model. Our research showed that there is no desert around low-mass stars, with a ratio of observed to predicted planets consistently above 0.5 for planets of 5-20 Earth masses. The findings of our study contradict previous expectations that the desert would appear around smaller stars, with one possible explanation being that massive Neptune-like planets are simply harder to lose during the formation of higher-mass giants. Based on our results, we believe that the desert around low-mass stars may be more accurately represented by a boundary in log-space rather than linear space, with a subsequent re-examination of the dataset required. Additionally, we found that the inner boundary of the desert is not linear, with a shift towards longer periods as planet mass increases. Our research also revealed that the shape of the boundary can vary based on detection limits and bias, with a notable change in the boundary's slope below a certain CORALIE detection limit. The findings of our study highlight the importance of complete statistical samples in understanding the planet formation desert and the need for further research on the low-mass end of the desert. With ongoing and upcoming datasets, we may see a shift in the low-mass end of the desert's characteristics. With more precise data, the low-mass end of the desert may reveal valuable insights into its nature and the processes involved in planet formation. With exoplanet detection capabilities extending to smaller detection limits, the low-mass end of the desert may reveal valuable insights. It works by optimizing attention distribution using a global penalty for undesired focus shifts. Unlike existing methods that require complicated pre-training procedures or specific task-dependent parameters, TOUGH can be easily incorporated into existing attention models and does not demand additional training or hyper-parameter tuning. We demonstrate the effectiveness of TOUGH through its impressive performance in both the study of attention behavior and real-world application in question answering, especially when dealing with highly diverse datasets like WikiQA. TOUGH's strengths include its ability to regulate attention harshness, promote more structured focus arrangements, and facilitate easier attention interpretation. When a and $\omega$ are close, the scalar fields exhibit Compton wave behavior, resulting in an effective potential and interaction mediating mechanisms similar to Yukawa. This yields a $1/r^2$ force, albeit much weaker than electromagnetic interactions, and an interaction range comparable to the dark matter particle mass. This property becomes significant for darker masses, leading to observable consequences at larger scales. Consequently, even lighter dark matter particles can produce observable self-interaction effects, potentially impacting structure formation assumptions. This research focuses on the macroscopic properties of compressed dark matter, specifically its self-gravity, equilibrium configurations, and particle collisions. Parameters derived from a specific model - including a dark matter self-interaction parameter $(\Gamma/\rho) \sim 10^{-11}-10^{-8}$ erg s cm-3, and a self-gravity parameter $(\Gamma/c^2) \sim 10^{-10}-10^{-7}$ erg s cm-3 - suggest a continuum from collisionless to hydrodynamic behavior. To further investigate, a simplified hydrodynamic model is developed to demonstrate how compressed dark matter can exhibit diverse macroscopic properties based on its particle mass and concentration. Specifically, a near-kinematic equilibrium can emerge due to the dark matter ensemble's non-Newtonian gravitational attraction. This can result in apparently moving masses with lower and higher kinetic energies relative to their counterparts in collisionless systems. By adjusting the dark matter particle mass and concentration, various macroscopic behavior can be replicated, including static and dynamic states. Moreover, a simplified hydrodynamic model is proposed to describe the dynamics of compressed dark matter without specifying its fundamental properties. By assuming a spatially homogeneous and isotropic system, the simplified model can effectively replicate a macroscopic equation similar to the Navier-Stokes equation, which can be applied to systems where the Compton wavelength is comparable to or larger than the system size. Consequently, even lighter compressed dark matter particles can produce observable self-gravity effects, potentially impacting structure formation assumptions. Based on a simplified hydrodynamic model, a general description of compressed dark matter dynamics is obtained, which can be applied to systems where the Compton wavelength is comparable to or larger than the system size. In a complex environment with unpredictable outcomes, an agent must adapt its behavior to achieve a predetermined level of success, a challenge akin to winning a lottery with long odds. We've developed a simple recurrent neural network design that accelerates learning in this environment, with a notable advantage: the faster learning rate is directly proportional to the cognitive task's complexity, not its level of difficulty. Through experimentation, our proposed architecture outperformed more sophisticated models in a variety of tasks, including navigation, predicting dynamic patterns, and solving grid-world problems. By leveraging a straightforward method to establish sparse connections between neurons, we uncovered a hidden mechanism that enhances learning: the formation of a localized information flow pattern, or "cluster," within the network. Within this cluster, information rapidly exchanges among neurons, facilitating rapid learning. In contrast, task-specific information tends to accumulate slowly outside this cluster, often irrelevant or inaccurate information. By localized learning, our method achieves faster adaptation, with notable benefits when applying it to challenging multi-task environments. The findings provide insights into the underlying biology of cognitive processes, sparking a new hypothesis: the sparsity of neurobiological circuits might be directly linked to the success in adapting to a complex environment. The study also investigates the characteristics of the tensor categories of linear representations. Active galactic nuclei with intense radio signals are among the most powerful celestial objects observable from Earth. Their high-energy emissions travel through the cosmic environment, affecting the development of galaxy clusters and the cosmic microwave background. A recent study in [1] examined the impact of relativistic jets from these objects on the cosmic background radiation, focusing on how it would change as the age of the universe increases. To further this research, we investigate how these jets influence the growth of supermassive black holes in the early universe and how this in turn affects the cosmic background radiation. Our findings reveal that, compared to present-day rates, the energy output of these black holes in the early universe could be millions of times greater. This increased energy output would primarily come from the kinetic energy of electrons as they interact with each other and other particles, forming a hard X-ray spectrum that also affects the cosmic background radiation. Similar to [1], we employ a self-regulating model for black hole growth, but with an added consideration for how relativistic jets impact the surrounding intergalactic medium. By calculating the energy exchanged between the black hole and its surroundings, we find that at a redshift of 1000 the energy exchanged is approximately 2% of the black hole's total mass energy. This percentage increases as the redshift grows, peaking at a redshift of 3000. A considerable portion of the exchanged energy takes the form of high-frequency radiation, accounting for a significant portion of the black hole's luminosity. This increased radiation could lead to an accelerated expansion of the black hole's accretion disk and a more intense emission of radiation from the black hole and its surroundings, resulting in an intensified feedback effect on the cosmic background radiation. Ultimately, our research suggests that relativistic jets from AGNs may have a more profound impact on the cosmic background radiation at the earliest stages of the universe than previously estimated. This effect, while temporary, could be several orders of magnitude greater than the jet power predicted by present-day values, ultimately decaying as the universe ages. Conversely, our research may provide an innovative explanation for the observed anomalies in the cosmic background radiation, including the intrinsic luminosity of black holes and their jets, as well as the equation of state of the ionized intergalactic medium. We introduce specific novel methods that simplify the process of combining estimation and segmentation, allowing both tasks to be performed simultaneously from unlabelled images. Notably, our proposed joint training approach surpasses existing domain adaptation methods, achieving improved performance in unsupervised domain adaptation applications. Generating engaging stories from time-series data poses a significant challenge, primarily due to the inherent sequence structure and the scarcity of relevant input features, which necessitate the inclusion of key events and their temporal relationships. Existing neural story generation methods often overlook these challenges, instead relying on model-specific configurations and story templates that limit their flexibility and domain applicability. To address these issues, we present TCube, a novel approach based on the Transformer model, designed to generate coherent and entertaining stories from diverse time-series datasets without requiring pre-defined templates. TCube integrates a novel event selection module, allowing it to determine the optimal number of events and incorporate multiple key events per segment, as well as enhance story coherence through contextualized event embeddings. Our experiments on three distinct datasets demonstrate TCube's superiority over state-of-the-art baselines in terms of both story coherence and engagement. Moreover, we highlight TCube's ability to adapt to various domains through a comprehensive ablation study. To further showcase TCube's capabilities, we have made available a wide range of generated stories across different domains. Additionally, the TCube repository includes open-source implementation details, allowing easy replication of our results. Further details are available at: https://whai-ai.github.io/TCube.

This research presents a novel neural network model for Japanese word division, leveraging the widely used JMdict dictionary. A unique, extended short-term memory architecture is employed to process the complex, morphologically driven nature of Japanese words. By incorporating a hidden layer with ReLU activation and a long short-term memory (LSTM) layer, the model is able to draw upon contextual information within the word and its surrounding neighbors. Due to the linguistic characteristics of Japanese, where a single character can represent multiple sounds, the model is designed to process input as a combination of hiragana, katakana, and kanji characters. A key feature of this model is its ability to read from left to right and incorporate contextual context, unlike previous Japanese word division systems that rely heavily on statistical methods. Although the model shows promising results, it is still plagued by issues of bias in the training data, as well as a limited understanding of part-of-speech specific grammatical variations. To mitigate these issues, a constrained model is introduced, which uses only JMdict dictionary definitions to guide the division process. This constrained model is evaluated under blind conditions and achieves a score of 90.4%, outperforming the unconstrained model and previous systems. Furthermore, using a word alignment technique, the division process is analyzed and suggestions are provided to improve the quality of JMdict dictionary definitions. Based on these findings, potential improvements are suggested for future models, including the integration of syntactic division methodologies. To facilitate easy use of the models, a web-based demonstration is made available for demonstration and testing purposes. Additionally, the source code used in this study is made available on GitHub. To evaluate the models, a new evaluation metric is introduced, specifically designed for Japanese word division tasks. This metric, known as the word division distance, measures the similarity between two division sets, and is particularly effective for tasks involving partial matches. Using this distance metric, the quality of JMdict dictionary definitions is analyzed, and certain issues are highlighted, such as the presence of incorrect readings. Consequently, the word division distance could be a valuable tool in assessing the quality of Japanese dictionary definitions. To confirm this, a blind evaluation is conducted using the word division distance metric, and the results reveal a significant improvement in the models' performance. The purpose of this study is to examine external links shared on Stack Overflow to gain insight into developers' preferences for online resources. Through a content analysis of 255,307 relevant questions and answers on Stack Overflow, we identified 21% that included an external link. Following a ranking of the top 100 most frequently cited domains based on their popularity, we gathered sufficient data for further investigation on 46 of them. Our analysis reveals that links sharing resources are often prefered over links promoting marketing or news. Interestingly, links to YouTube, GitHub, and Bitcoin Wallet are preferred by developers over links to news outlets, social media, and financial services. Furthermore, we observed a significant preference (75%) for links to web services that require authentication, suggesting that developers often prefer to access protected content via a single trusted platform. Our findings provide valuable insights for developers and programmers who frequently utilize external links and aim to create useful knowledge bases for others. These insights can also aid in solving the problem of link rot, a common issue affecting the durability of knowledge-based data. We intend to conduct further research based on the preferences demonstrated in this study, focusing on exploring the underlying reasons behind these preferences in the near future. Data for this study can be accessed via this link: https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.fbcs.2022.11.002.ensemble.101.

Our team conducted a thorough evaluation of current galaxy light measurement techniques used to extract galaxy distance information from supernovae data, taking into account time variability. We assessed the potential of these solutions to accurately calculate galaxy luminosity, suppress supernovae data noise, and remain unbiased throughout the process. From our examination, we identified key characteristics that allow a solution to yield precise distance measurements: (1) the solution must accurately model the galaxy's emission, (2) it must effectively remove noise, (3) it should incorporate active learning to optimize data utilization, (4) it must remain free of biases, and (5) it should consistently apply to all galaxy types. By following the order in which these characteristics typically appear in scientific discussions, we presented an overview of the current state of solutions used in the supernovae community, used these characteristics to guide an in-depth analysis of each, and through mock data testing, we demonstrated the superiority of certain methods in recovering the galaxy's emission spectrum and suppressing noisy data points. Our study revealed that while some methods excel at recovering the galaxy's emission spectrum, they may perform poorly in suppressing noise, and vice versa. Notably, we found that the task of removing noisy data points is inherently linked to the goal of calculating the galaxy's emission spectrum, and suppressing noise is crucial in ensuring accurate distance measurements. Consequently, we recommend employing multiple approaches to galaxy estimation and comparing their performance on mock data tailored to resemble real observations, and subsequently, selecting the solution with the best overall performance. Furthermore, we emphasize the importance of developing a comprehensive understanding of the solutions' limitations and strengths, and the need for future work in exploring active learning and noise suppression techniques. Ultimately, we conclude that while some solutions may yield accurate distance measurements even with noisy data, other methods may require high-quality data but may fail to do so, and therefore, we must continue to improve these solutions used in the calculation of galaxy distances from supernovae data. This research is an effort to provide clarity on the current state of solutions used in the supernovae data analysis and their properties, and it is essential that future work relies on this foundational understanding. This way, we can ensure that our future work, such as mock data generation for future surveys, does not repeat past mistakes and is guided by a comprehensive understanding of the galaxy variability problem. This research can serve as a foundational paper for future work in active learning and noise suppression techniques. This work is an effort to contribute to a broader goal of determining the cosmological constant through supernovae data

To combat climate change, global cooperation is crucial, yet frequently hindered by country-specific obstacles, clear consequences, and reliable international data. We propose a comprehensive climate database, answering which countries are responsible for the problem, what damage will result from inaction, and what benefits can be reaped from cooperation. Medical condition diagnosis via clinical note analysis is hindered because notes are specific to particular hospitals and are often written in specialized medical terminology. To address this challenge, researchers employed Domain Generalization (DG) by creating a model that uses information from hospital-specific notes to generate informed responses about medical symptoms across various domains. In this paper, we take a different approach and focus on whether the underlying general model can recognize relevant symptom information from different domains. To this end, we propose a new benchmark called Symptom Extraction by Oversampling Irrelevant data with Negation (SEION), which consists of extensive datasets containing medical symptoms expressed in different ways and contexts. The SEION benchmark includes two separate sections: one that tests the ability to extract symptoms in a specific hospital setting, and another that evaluates the ability to extract symptoms in entirely new, unseen domains. Building on this benchmark, we developed FastText-based models for both domains, and through thorough experimentation, we demonstrated the efficacy of our proposed model and the SEION benchmark in promoting DG for symptom extraction. To our knowledge, this is the first time a DG benchmark focused on extracting symptoms has been established. The dataset and model code are publicly available for research purposes. Furthermore, we observed in our experiments that incorporating negation and contradiction markers in hospital notes often leads to contrasting outcomes in different domains. For instance, the symptom 'high blood pressure' is beneficial in one domain, whereas it is detrimental in another. This discovery highlights the complexities involved in interpreting medical symptom information in different contexts, and it also suggests that the interplay between symptoms may vary significantly across different domains, further emphasizing the need for DG in medical symptom extraction. As a result, the generated model can be a valuable ally to clinicians in developing more comprehensive systems for medical condition diagnosis. To ensure the robustness of our method, we plan to investigate the following areas in the future: first, developing a DG model that can effectively integrate knowledge from various hospital notes; second, designing an automated system for selecting relevant hospital notes that can generalize well to other domains. By addressing these challenges, we aim to create a more robust DG model for symptom extraction. To sum up, we presented a new DG benchmark called SEION, and through thorough research, we demonstrated the complexity of interpreting medical symptom information in different domains. Furthermore, we observed the potential of fastText models in promoting DG for symptom extraction. Lastly, we outlined our future research plans to further enhance our proposed DG approach. To ensure reproducibility, we have publicly shared our dataset and model code for the research community

reinforcement learning to train an autonomous vehicle. The autonomous vehicle

navigate from a starting point to a designated endpoint while avoiding
obstacles. The model employs an open-source 3D simulator called New York
City Simulator, which provides a realistic environment that an agent can
interact with. Furthermore, the model leverages a deep reinforcement learning

vehicle tests. To validate the model's performance, it successfully completed
tests in three diverse scenarios: navigating through city streets, avoiding
construction zones, and adapting to traffic lights. The model's source code is
publicly available on GitHub.

This research investigates the thermodynamic characteristics of quark stars composed entirely of spin-aligned strange quarks, in the presence of an external magnetic field. We employed the MIT bag model to calculate the energy density and pressure of these quarks and then evaluated how they respond to temperature variations. Furthermore, we were able to derive an equation that governs the thermodynamic speed of these quark stars as a function of temperature, radius, and specific energy density. Our analysis also enables the calculation of specific heat, entropy, and Helmholz free energy. We further developed a theoretical model to examine the impact of a strong magnetic field on quark star structure, using the TOV equations. Our results demonstrate that in the presence of a strong magnetic field, the mass radius relation of the quark star undergoes significant alterations. Specifically, as the magnetic field increases, the radius of the quark star decreases. Consequently, this is accompanied by a rise in the maximum mass the quark star can support. Like conventional stars, the thermodynamic properties of quark stars also exhibit significant changes at the critical temperature of deconfinement. Pando is a novel decentralized, peer-to-peer computing platform that enables the creation of general-purpose, grid-scale volunteer crowds. Built on top of WebRTC and WebSockets, Pando allows users to integrate custom applications quickly, leveraging a user-friendly browser-based interface and a visual flow-based workflow. Pando relies on an implicit consensus mechanism, where users' preferences are considered equal, and no trust is required for maintaining the network's integrity. We evaluated Pando through two distinct scenarios: a simulated network test and a real-world deployment, demonstrating its efficacy and outlining suggestions for future improvements. Pando is now open-source, accessible at https://pando.cc/. Developers are welcome to explore and contribute to this platform. Additionally, a demo showcasing Pando's capabilities is available at https://pando-demo.cc/. Feel free to visit the demo site, create an account, and experience Pando firsthand.

We introduce a nonparametric estimation procedure for a nonlinear eigenvalue problem that involves a spectral density with well-known smoothness. To achieve this, we first create an orthonormal basis adapted to a nonlinear operator corresponding to the eigenvalue problem, and then use this basis to estimate the spectral density through a minimal rational interpolation method. By doing so, we obtain an $L^2$-convergence rate of $\lambda n^{-\alpha/(2\alpha+1)}$, where $\alpha$ represents the smoothness, up to a factor dependent on the degree of the interpolation. This result improves upon existing estimation procedures for nonlinear spectral analysis that often require a higher degree of interpolation. However, the price paid is increased computational complexity. This study showcases the first adaptive estimation procedure for a nonlinear eigenvalue problem in a nonparametric setting. To obtain the convergence rate, we utilize a uniform convergence result for eigenfunctions and also address the issue of estimating eigenvalues. Notably, the method can be extended to multivariate spectral analysis. Ultimately, extensive numerical experiments are conducted to demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed procedure. In this research, we investigate the properties of $SO(N_c)$ gauge theories, specifically ${\cal N}=1$ and ${\cal N}=2$ super Yang-Mills theories, when formulated in a three-dimensional (3D) semi-space with boundaries. We demonstrate the existence of a boundary phase shift, bound state formation, and chiral symmetry disruption due to boundary interactions. The phase shifts of $SU(N_c)$ and $SO(N_c)$ theories differ significantly, especially in the number and depth of their phases. Additionally, we discuss how these phases in $SO(N_c)$ theories can be linked to those of $SU(N_c)$ theories through dualities. A crucial aspect of this research involves analyzing a boundary condition modification that introduces a supersymmetric quantum mechanics (SQM) module on each boundary, which influences the number and depth of the phases, especially in multi-bounded systems. The SQM module introduces an additional degree of freedom, thus altering the phase structure entirely. Notably, this research provides an original example where an $SO(N_c)$ gauge theory exhibits a richer phase structure compared to its $SU(N_c)$ counterpart. Ultimately, we present a systematic approach to determining the phase structure of quiver gauge theories based on their boundary quantum mechanics components. Additionally, this research offers a systematic understanding of chiral symmetry disruption and confinement in 3D semi-space systems. Furthermore, this research develops novel tools to analyze phase structures in gauge theories, which may have practical applications in the study of various quantum systems. Lastly, we discuss the possibility of experimental validation of our research through the creation of artificial magnetic materials inspired by boundary phases. Such an experiment could provide a tangible connection between our theoretical findings and real-world observations. Conversely, an experiment failing to replicate our predictions could offer an alternative explanation of our results. Moreover, this research demonstrates the intricate relationship between gauge theories and quantum mechanics, specifically supersymmetric quantum mechanics. The research can be extended to higher-dimensional systems by investigating the properties of gauge theories with boundaries in five and six dimensions. Furthermore, this research delves into the mathematical concepts underlying topological phases, specifically the role of instantons in 5D and (p,q) 6D gauge theories with boundaries. In federated learning, multiple parties collaborate on training machine learning models by sharing local parameters, rather than sensitive data. Despite this setup's security benefits, the process itself remains vulnerable to attacks, such as data poisoning and parameter tampering. To address these issues, we propose an novel approach, flatee, that utilizes Trusted Execution Environments to safeguard the training process. Specifically, each party's model is obfuscated and executed within a TEE, isolated from the outside environment. This TEE-based setup offers protection against attacks like data poisoning and parameter tampering, by encrypting and encrypting the model, even when accessed. Furthermore, to ensure data privacy during training, we leverage the TEE to apply secure transformations, such as homomorphic encryption, in a way that only permits encrypted computations, without exposing the data. Through comprehensive experiments, our solution has shown equivalent or better performance, when compared to existing techniques, showcasing at least 10% improvement in test accuracy, using fewer iterations. Moreover, the benefits of using TEEs extend to significant energy savings, with up to 60% reduced energy consumption, measured as power flux. These findings confirm that using TEEs offers a viable and efficient solution, to safeguard the federated learning process, while providing robust security and performance. Modern microservice applications consist of many containerized processes communicating with each other through system calls. Traditional security frameworks focused on individual process behavior fall short when addressing more complex attacks involving multiple processes. In response, researchers have proposed various system call denials policies but implementing them is impractical due to the static nature of denial policies. To address this, a dynamic approach, known as call control, allows for real-time decision-making but is typically tailored to specific applications. This gives an attacker leverage to manipulate system calls to enable security breaches. To address the need for efficient and scalable security solutions, we propose a novel approach called Timeloops, capable of automatically generating call control policies for any microservice application through learning. This is achieved by analyzing system call patterns, leveraging pre-existing libraries, and using a data structure to store common patterns. This allows Timeloops to provide efficient and scalable security, even in complex and large-scale applications. Our current implementation, which supports Linux-based x86-64 system calls, is capable of achieving performance comparable to state-of-the-art microservice security solutions while achieving a speedup of up to 3 times over traditional system call denial policies. This is achieved through a range of features including memory scope, performance scope, and controller pooling. To facilitate a deeper understanding, we provide a timely-based representation of system call patterns and explain the underlying reasoning behind our approach. Through extensive testing on diverse benchmarks, including the Open-source Thermopyles benchmark, a dynamic denial-of-service benchmark, and five real-world microservice applications, our results demonstrate the efficacy of Timeloops in achieving substantial speedups, reducing overhead, and preventing security breaches. Our findings highlight the practical value of Timeloops in real-world microservice applications, emphasizing the need for further research in system call learning. This leads to numerous avenues for future research and development, encouraging the extension of Timeloops to other denial policy types, integration with existing security frameworks, and exploration of new features in system call learning. By promoting a more scalable and flexible approach to system call control, Timeloops has the potential to contribute significantly to the security of microservice applications. To facilitate this, we release Timeloops as an open-source project, providing a wide range of features and functionality to the community. This enables researchers and developers to build upon our work, testing Timeloops on various use cases and evaluating its performance in real-world settings. Researchers distinguish between two categories of stellar arrangements: a simple pattern where stars conform to well-defined orbits and a more complex scenario where orbital paths overlap extensively. This paper introduces a cutting-edge approach called Random Model Predictive Control, which utilizes machine learning and optimal control techniques in a unified manner. By generating multiple models through random parameterization, we can identify models that are robust to changes in system parameters. Applying the Random Model Predictive Control algorithm to a predetermined set of models, we can generate control inputs that minimize performance costs while ensuring the system remains within desired boundaries. Notably, our method does not require extensive computational efforts to determine the number of models, as increasing the number of models directly results in reduced computation costs and improved closed-loop robustness performance. This concept is illustrated through simulation experiments involving a basic variable structure control system. This study offers an original approach to addressing the challenges posed by uncertain system parameters in non-linear control systems. To analyze the dynamics of species competition, we developed an intricate model, an intrinsically chaotic version of the voter model that incorporates a competition-colonization tradeoff. This model indicates that a diverse community with numerous species can persist indefinitely, whereas a system with only a few large species will eventually decline. Our model reveals two distinct mechanisms contributing to the coexistence of various species: the stabilization of patterns through trade-off interactions and the potential for one species to dominate another through colonization, leading to species replacement. By employing both theoretical and numerical methods, we explored the model's interior and boundary dynamics, ultimately determining that the model exhibits two distinct transition points in its parameter space - an -phase transition and a Hopf bifurcation - which separately give rise to periodic and chaotic patterns. This research demonstrates that the interplay between species movement, interaction, and trade-offs can give rise to a variety of intricate patterns in species distribution, ultimately leading to the coexistence of diverse species through the colonization of one species within another's habitat. Depending on the species' trade-off and migration strategies, these communities can become more organized or even more complex, presenting novel patterns of life. Interestingly, the model's parameter space is divided into three distinct regions, each corresponding to a different type of community dynamics - monomorphic (single-species) communities, communities with a dominant species and various sub-dominant species, and diverse communities with numerous coexisting species. Lastly, our findings also shed light on the connections between species distribution patterns, the species' trade-off strategy, and the species' fitness, offering insights into the relationship between these factors in the coexistence of diverse species communities. This research provides a theoretical foundation for the diversity of life on Earth, presenting various patterns of species organization and the intricate community dynamics that can result from the interaction of different species strategies. Additionally, the models and findings presented here can be applied to the analysis of various ecological systems, such as islands with colonizing species, and may also have relevance beyond biology, potentially influencing the understanding of social dynamics in sociology and the development of algorithms in computer science. Lastly, our research demonstrates the diversity of patterns that can arise within the dynamics of ecological systems and the importance of considering species trade-offs in the understanding of community dynamics and diversity. Neron Desingularization of one-dimensional local rings, and this algorithm
involves a series of specific transformations, each of which can be applied universally
and also satisfies certain additional conditions. This algorithm is then used to
prove the excellence of one-dimensional local rings and also establish the Neron
Desingularization for such rings under the presence of excellence in the base ring.
Furthermore, several key properties of the Neron Desingularization, such as its
uniqueness and monic property, are proved independently of excellence in the base
ring. This algorithm is comparable to M. Artin, J. Tate, and T. Shimura's algorithm
for the completion of one-dimensional local rings, and we provide a comprehensive
survey of comparisons with other desingularization algorithms, including
M. Artin's, A. Grothendieck's, and M. Raynaud's works. Additionally, several
examples and counterexamples are provided to illustrate the significance and
limitations of the excellent closure property in the context of one-dimensional local
rings. This research provides a thorough rewriting and expansion of the author's 2009
Ph.D. dissertation, and it is an extension of the dissertation's primary content,
while also incorporating several supplementary results and examples. This research is
presented in a manner that is accessible to Ph.D. students and advanced researchers in
related fields. We assume a solid understanding of basic local cohomology and also
include numerous proofs and detailed explanations to support this requirement. 
Finally, this research is an expression of the author's gratitude to the
institutions and individuals who provided essential support during the research. 
Notably, this research is an expression of the author's gratitude to the University
of California at Berkeley, where the research was conducted, as well as to the
influence of the research's main advisors, S. Kemp and P. Schenzel. Moreover, this
research is an expression of the author's gratitude to numerous other researchers and
institutions, as listed in Section 0.3, and also to the anonymous referees for their

This study utilizes a Laser Doppler Velocimeter (LDV) to acquire two-dimensional flow data around a sphere in a fluid. Due to the single-point nature of traditional LDV systems, we develop an innovative, automated method to efficiently gather 2D measurements by strategically moving the LDV in a predetermined pattern. This approach enables the collection of a full set of 2D velocity data within a reasonable time frame, facilitating the acquisition of two-dimensional flow data. We present a detailed analysis of our experimental setup, the automated movement system, and the resulting 2D flow data. To validate our technique, we compare its findings with existing experimental data for a sphere in a specific fluid at a particular Reynolds number, and we also examine the effect of varying an important experimental parameter. Our research demonstrates that this automated method can provide high-quality 2D flow data similar to that obtained by a 2D LDV system at a significantly lower cost to the user. We estimate that our system can collect the same data in approximately 12% of the time required by a 2D LDV system for the specific conditions examined. Additionally, we provide a method for estimating the uncertainty associated with our measurements. We believe that our automated technique will contribute to the widespread use of single-point LDV systems in experimental fluid mechanics research. With further refinement, this approach may also be applied to other types of experimental setups. We plan to share our findings with the public, and the associated data will be made available. However, controlling a phase object of this nature proves to be a complex task. Simulation outcomes reveal that while a phase disc can contribute to focusing electrons with higher order sagittals, its influence is largely dependent on the specific sample structure and its placement. Consequently, we propose that a phase disc should not be solely relied upon for astigmatization correction but rather be used in conjunction with existing techniques. Additionally, we suggest that a multi-disc approach, featuring multiple programmable phases, may offer superior performance in improving resolution and contrast, particularly at high spatial frequencies. Finally, we outline potential design considerations for an experimental setup that could effectively modulate a phase disc via a laser beam, thus requiring rapid control over the phase disc pattern at millisecond or sub-millisecond intervals. Such an system could potentially be integrated within an existing TEM apparatus to evaluate our theoretical predictions in practical scenarios. Ultimately, this study provides a comprehensive foundation for designing an experimental setup that could effectively utilize a phase disc as an dynamic element within an electron microscope, thereby enabling the temporal modulation of electron phase and the subsequent impact on its focus. Lastly, we suggest exploring the potential of employing devices that modulate a phase disc through a laser beam to tackle challenging applications in optics and physics. Our framework is based on an analytical solution to the Bogoliubov-de Gennes equations for graphene's electronic Hamiltonian, incorporating the effects of Coulomb interactions through a self-consistent approximation. This approach allows us to derive an exact analytical formula for the specific heat capacity of graphene, which we validated by comparing it with numerical simulations from the Princeton University Materials Computation Group's software. Our results show that this self-consistent approximation is equivalent to the RPA solution for low energy levels, and that by varying the energy cutoff in the Coulomb potential, we can observe the transition from weakly coupled graphene to graphene islands. Recent advances in end-to-end text-to-speech systems based on neural networks have led to significant improvements in speech synthesis performance. However, synthesizing high-quality dialogue with a long context and non-consecutive text remains a major challenge due to network capacity limitations. To address this issue, a novel approach called MaskedDialogue is proposed, which integrates a masking technique with existing top-down attention mechanisms in sequence-to-sequence models. By selectively masking input dialogue tokens, MaskedDialogue enables the network to focus on crucial words, thereby producing more coherent and natural-sounding speech. Experimental results on the Dialog corpora demonstrate that MaskedDialogue outperforms baseline systems in various metrics, including human evaluation. Code and demo are available on GitHub. The researchers developed a relevant dataset by simulating IEEE 802.11p channel properties based on 2D Raleigh fading, and split it into training and testing sections. Notably, the CaLSTM model, an LSTM variant enhanced with causal elements, demonstrates superior predictive capabilities in this application. Comprehensive evaluations of the proposed method's resilience, parameter sensitivity, and its comparison with other leading techniques, further validate its effectiveness. The researchers also analyzed the influence of vehicle speed and channel length on the method's accuracy. The study concludes by highlighting the advantages and limitations of this approach, and encouraging its use as a robust tool for vehicular communication system design. We introduce a novel approach to automatic neural network design, drawing inspiration from information theory. Unlike traditional methods that rely on gradient backpropagation, our method proactively develops an optimal network architecture by estimating a regulatory parameter through a universal expectation-maximization process. This process begins with a preliminary approximation of the model's parameters, after which we implement the Sharpening Effect to analyze entropy. By applying Bayes' theorem, we derive a closed-form expression for the expected free energy, facilitating the estimation of our primary parameter. Notably, this method is unspecific to the type of loss function used, instead relying on information theory principles alone. Consequently, our method is more robust and adaptable, enabling seamless extension to complex scenarios involving multiple parameters and non-differentiable components. The method's efficacy is demonstrated in a range of experiments, where we show that it is capable of developing an optimal neural network architecture for diverse data sets. The code for this approach is available on GitHub at the following address: https://github.com/ArmanZandaghi/Information-Theoretic-ANN-Design. The data used in our experiments can be accessed via the following links: https://armanzandaghi.github.io/Information-Theoretic-ANN-Data. In addition, we have performed an open evaluation of our method using real-world EEG data, specifically in the context of P300-based BCI applications. The concept of metastructures that operate at multiple frequencies has become increasingly popular in recent research, spanning areas such as acoustic, sound waves and optics. While they have shown great potential in manipulating energy at various scales, the design of these structures often lacks a unified approach that can efficiently handle input signals and guide energy across different frequency ranges. To address this gap, we propose a general framework for designing dual-frequency metastructures based on a combination of wave resonance and phase matching principles. We begin by exploring the theoretical foundations of our approach, which involves matching the resonant frequencies of individual subunits through phase locking. To demonstrate the efficacy of our methodology, we prototype and numerically investigate two dual-frequency metastructures - one designed for sound waves and the other for the terahertz spectrum. The experimental results show that our designs can effectively guide energy across both the 1.5 GHz and 6 THz frequency ranges with high efficiency. We anticipate that our phase matching technique will have a significant impact on the development of innovative technologies in acoustic, sound wave and terahertz applications. With its broad applicability, this approach can be easily adapted for other frequency ranges including optics. In fact, we have successfully incorporated a simple geometric metamaterial strategy to guide light through photonic dual-metallic structures, achieving remarkable results. We are confident that our work will inspire novel ideas in photonic research and contribute to the advancement of this field. Additionally, we provide comprehensive supporting details, including tables and figures, that highlight our design solutions, numerical modeling and analysis, and experimental verification. These supplementary details can be found at the following link: https://doi.org/10.6084/m9f10-1831. We look forward to seeing the numerous ways in which our research will stimulate new developments in the research community. Tb3RuO7 exhibits an unusual 5-fold coordination environment, which is uncommon in magnetolectric materials. This unique feature, along with the presence of Ru ions in a 2+ state, prevents the material from displaying an antiferromagnetic arrangement. Instead, it features a unique 1/2 and 1 configuration in the Ru chains, which arises from the disorder of the neighboring Tb ions. This peculiar state places Tb3RuO7 in an exclusive category among the magnetolectric materials, rendering detailed magnetic and transport measurements indispensable to fully comprehend its behavior and properties. This study leverages single-crystal and powder X-ray diffraction, as well as SQUID and muon spin resonance ($\mu$SR) analysis to map out the magnetic domain structure and examine the material's low-temperature spin dynamics. This research presents M-ar-K-Rapid, a high-performance implementation of the Fast Centralized Independent Component Analysis (Fast ICA) algorithm, optimized for running on accelerator cards such as GPUs and FPGAs. By leveraging these accelerators, M-ar-K-Rapid achieves significant speedup gains on large-scale parallel computing platforms. Additionally, we have developed a flexible and dynamic software framework that allows for the deployment of ICA-based neural network learning algorithm on accelerator cards. This flexibility enables support for various algorithmic variants derived from Fast ICA, as well as the integration of these algorithms within bigger learning paradigms such as deep learning. Extensive experimental evaluations have demonstrated that M-ar-Rapid consistently obtains the highest level of acceleration performance compared to other existing ICA algorithm implementations on GPUs and FPGAs. Furthermore, we have found that our implementation can be up to 7 times faster than current CPU-based ICA algorithms, while still maintaining accurate results comparable to benchmark CPU standards. Specifically, our tests have shown that M-ar-K-Rapid yields average acceleration rates of 2.4 times and 3.5 times on GPUs and FPGAs, respectively, across a wide range of various ICA algorithms. Moreover, although our accelerator-based approach might introduce minor accuracy losses of around 0.3%, it significantly outperforms conventional CPU-based methods by at least 6.3 times. Finally, we have successfully applied M-ar-K-Rapid in several complex computing tasks such as face recognition and classification tasks within the MNIST and CIFAR10 datasets, thereby showcasing its potential for use in various ICA algorithm applications. Overall, the integration of ICA learning algorithms onto accelerator cards such as GPUs and FPGAs, facilitated by our software framework, has led to the development of novel learning paradigms that could be useful in future research. Moreover, the successful deployment of ICA algorithms onto general-purpose parallel computing platforms may open up new avenues for accelerating a wide range of learning-based applications. early detection of issues in the development process of a program. However, 
unverified assertions remaining in the code can hinder the compilation process 
at any stage of the program's development cycle. This paper examines the causes 
and categorizes the types of unverified assertions that cause complications in 
compilation, also outlining a framework called Paraffin that employs static code 
analysis to locate and resolve unverified assertions during the compilation process. 
By categorizing unverified assertions into three types and utilizing a framework, 
developers can employ specific strategies to handle each case, ensuring that unverified 
assertions do not introduce inconsistencies into the program's codebase. 
Empirical evaluations and case studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of this 
approach in an industry-based setting. Specifically, the proposed method has been 
tested on the Apache Software Foundation's projects and a set of open-source Java 
libraries, yielding a success rate of over 90% in handling unverified assertions.

assertions across various categories within the tested codebases. To facilitate

The surge in social media usage has led to an abundance of geotagged data, which has enabled researchers to develop methods for spatio-temporal incident detection. We contend that traditional detection methods, which rely on predefined incident types and incident density thresholds, are insufficient because they fail to account for varying incident forms and densities. In response, we present a novel instantaneous spatio-temporal incident identification approach, which employs real-time analytics and machine learning algorithms to automatically detect incidents from streaming geotagged social media data. We propose an incident density ratio model that leverages support vector machines, providing a discriminative and flexible solution for incident characterization. Furthermore, our approach incorporates the Farthest Neighbor algorithm for optimal regression boundary fitting and density estimation. Experimental evaluations conducted on public datasets demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed method, which surpasses traditional techniques in accuracy and incident representation diversity. Notably, our method achieves a recall of 0.9, along with an accuracy of 0.8 for incident replication, and provides meaningful density ratios with up to 95% relevance to incident types. These outstanding results validate the utility of our approach for real-world instant incident detection and analysis. For example, our method can identify incidents, such as concerts and festivals, which may not be detected through pre-defined types or density analysis. We envision that our approach will contribute to the development of more sophisticated incident detection methods, enabling various social media analytics applications in the future. Details of our method are available on GitHub at https://github.com/AmrYossef/Instantaneous-STIID. This research investigates typical dissemination patterns of online rumors in China by analyzing COVID-19-related information shared on Weibo, a prominent Chinese micro-blogging platform. We selected four critical phases of the epidemic period and examined the characteristics of online rumors, including their source types, propagation patterns, and impact on public sentiment. We also developed a model to measure the influence of a rumor by tracking its spread through multiple social networks. The results show that a small number of highly malicious rumors were responsible for the greatest spread and most significant impact on public sentiment, which was exacerbated by their association with violence and health concerns. The findings can inform the design of an algorithmic system to detect and mitigate the dissemination of online rumors in China. Additionally, the study's insights can be applied to better understand the dynamics of misinformation spread during crises and inform crisis communication strategies by governments to effectively counter rumors with official information. Remote sensing imagery is a vital data type that has far-reaching applications in various fields such as urban planning, environmental monitoring, and geology. The extensive range of pixels within remote sensing images, which vary by wavelength, is known as hyperspectral images. Current deep learning methods often employ convolutional neural networks (CNN) to analyze these images, typically utilizing a fixed number of spectral dimensions when classifying pixels. Nevertheless, it has been demonstrated in this research that reducing the number of spectral dimensions can affect hyperspectral pixel classification, and different networks may react differently to such dimensionality reduction. A dataset containing samples from various types of remote sensing imagery was used to investigate the influence of dimensionality reduction on hyperspectral pixel classification, and the findings revealed significant variations in classification accuracy across different networks and dimensionality reduction methods. The study also demonstrated the feasibility of employing spectral dimensionality reduction methods to enhance the performance of traditional CNN-based approaches, and potentially other deep learning methods, under specific conditions. Recent advances in natural language models have led to remarkable performance improvements, yet these models remain challenging to interpret, requiring substantial computational power to adjust even minor aspects of their architecture. In this context, our work aims to minimize the complexity of natural language models, making it possible to understand how modifications to their design impact overall results. Building upon existing research in model reduction techniques, such as the NTK approach, we develop novel methods to reduce neural language models based on linearization, dimensionality reduction, and contraction of model parameters. By applying these techniques, we achieve a reduction in the number of model parameters for models like Transformer and BERT by orders of magnitude, with minimal loss in accuracy on specific evaluation tasks. Moreover, our reduced models exhibit comparable results to the original large-scale models in downstream NLP tasks, as supported by empirical evidence. A novel method, referred to as ProCS-BMPS, has been introduced for de novo protein structure prediction or refining existing structures using amide proton chemical shifts obtained through quantum mechanics. ProCS-BMPS utilizes a simplified linear relation to predict chemical shifts, matching the accuracy of more complex relationships, while its statistical potential is designed to replicate the interactions of quantum mechanical fragments, specifically to replicate the non-covalent interactions of these fragments with amide protons. Tests of ProCS-BMPS have demonstrated a strong correlation with experimental data for a general protein fold, and the method has shown the ability to accurately place key residues in the binding site of rapamycin binding protein domain, using atomic resolution data for guidance. Additionally, ProCS-BMPS has been combined with ROSETTA's energy functions to validate and refine protein structures at a medium resolution level. These experiments have highlighted the potential of ProCS-BMPS to contribute to the development of more accurate protein structure prediction methods. Finally, ProCS-BMPS has been combined with ROSETTA's design mode to design protein variants with improved stability, and the results have shown a correlation between predicted chemical shifts and the stability of green fluorescent protein variants. Overall, ProCS-BMPS has been demonstrated to be an effective tool for the validation, refinement, and design of protein structures. Future work will involve the integration of ProCS-BMPS into the ROSETTA framework for general protein structure prediction and design. The code for ProCS-BMPS is available on the following GitHub repository: https://github.com/CompBioLabProtein/ProCS-BMPS. Recent studies have made substantial efforts to investigate the biases introduced by different loss functions in deep learning models. Nevertheless, there's a noticeable gap in the understanding of how loss function modifications affect models. This research aims to advance the knowledge on loss function bias by thoroughly examining the impact of utilizing the cross-entropy loss function with its modified variants, specifically for classification tasks. We focus on exploring loss function propagation throughout the model and its influence on both training and testing processes. In addition to this, we developed a theoretical framework to explain and predict the degree of loss function bias. The proposed framework, referred to as the Expected Label Fraction Hypothesis (ELFH), asserts that the average ratio of a model's correct predictions to its total predictions is a constant that remains unchanged under different loss function variations. We discovered through experiments that ELFH is capable of accurately estimating loss function bias and that this bias can be eliminated or reduced by utilizing techniques such as data augmentation, label stabilization, and ensemble modeling. Consequently, using these methods enables deep learning models to exhibit improved robustness to loss function modifications. Notably, combining these methods resulted in a model that exhibited superior performance on adversarially tested samples under both tabular data conditions and distributed dataset scenarios. We also studied the computational efficiency of these methods and found that they can be easily implemented with minimal additional computational requirements. Hence, using techniques such as data augmentation, label stabilization, and ensemble modeling to reduce loss function bias offers promising results. These findings suggest that these methods could be exploited by adversarial attackers to further deteriorate the robustness of deep learning models, potentially leading to significant performance declines of up to 9% as demonstrated through experiments. Therefore, it is crucial for model developers and users to be aware of the potential loss function bias and to take steps to mitigate its effects. Conversely, attackers may also benefit from understanding the dynamics of loss function modifications by adopting the ELFH strategy, which could result in improved methods for testing the robustness of deep learning models against adversarial attacks. A new perspective on parquet theory is offered through the incorporation of vertex corrections within a bare electron-gas structure.  The parquet approach is equivalently expressed through a rescaling of the four-point correlation function.  However, this may not always yield a minimal rescaling when applied to dense systems like metals.  The alternative method of incorporating vertex corrections is then described in terms of a molecular dynamics-like scheme that maintains a balance between electron propagation and local interaction.  The local interaction is divided into distinct components, each propagated in an imaginary time framework that is reversed to yield a negative time structure.  The conventional parquet approach is compared with this new perspective, with simulations conducted for a one-dimensional Hubbard model.  The results reveal notable differences between the two methodologies, particularly at low concentrations of electron interaction.  Notably, the molecular dynamics-like method exhibits convergence issues in the imaginary time structure, where convergence is more readily achieved with a time-dependent local interaction that is not present in the conventional parquet approach.  The comparison of energy vs. concentration of electron interaction for the two methodologies shows notable disparity at low concentrations, with the conventional parquet approach overestimating energy by a factor of up to two times the concentration of electron interaction.  In contrast, the molecular dynamics-like method exhibits lesser dependence on the structure of the rescaled four-point correlation function, with this dependence diminishing at lower concentrations of electron interaction.  The effect of local interaction breaking in the conventional parquet approach is identified as the primary source of difference, with this effect most pronounced at lower concentrations of electron interaction.  Lastly, the incorporation of vertex corrections within the molecular dynamics-like method is shown to yield a correct power-law behavior for the electronic self-energy at lower concentrations of electron interaction.  In contrast, the conventional parquet approach may yield sublinear power-law behavior for the electronic self-energy that contains nonlinear terms in the concentration of electron interaction.  Overall, the incorporation of vertex corrections within the molecular dynamics-like method is shown to be a more accurate approach for describing the electronic self-energy at lower concentrations of electron interaction.  Similarly, this methodology is expected to yield improved results for describing the dynamics of various optical coefficients in metals.  The comparison of energy vs. concentration of electron interaction for the one-dimensional Hubbard model is accompanied by corresponding observations for the two-dimensional Hubbard model, with the results showing notable similarity. To study the phenomenon of exciton liquefaction in 2D semiconductors, we have developed an ab initio theoretical framework which utilizes many-body perturbation theory to calculate exciton formation and interaction within a finite-size lattice. This approach allows us to determine whether a material exhibits exciton Bose-Einstein condensation, and we demonstrate its efficacy by applying it to the 2D material TiSe2. In this case, our simulations reveal the existence of strong electron-phonon coupling and charge density waves at low temperatures, and we find that exciton Bose-Einstein condensation does not occur due to overwhelming electron-phonon coupling coupling that leads to charge density waves. Moreover, we observe a significant shift in the energy spectrum of TiSe2 that is characteristic of superconducting materials. Additionally, we observe that the charge density waves in TiSe2 exhibit a correlation length of less than the finite-size lattice, and we find that the density of these waves is directly proportional to the energy released during their formation. Lastly, we observe that the charge density waves in TiSe2 exhibit self-organized criticality, and we suggest that this phenomenon provides a potential explanation for the recently-observed $q=\pi/a$ magnetic order in the material. Finally, we note that the excitonic effect plays a significant role in the strength of the electron-phonon coupling in TiSe2.

Emergency response systems play a vital role in safeguarding community safety. The process of dispatching emergency services begins with callers providing critical information, which is often overlooked in the dispatching process. This research aims to uncover the concealed meanings within verbal interactions between callers and dispatchers, which can improve the effectiveness of these systems. A notable example of such systems is the Beijing 119 system, which received over 1 million daily calls. A comprehensive dataset was compiled by analyzing transcripts of over 300,000 calls, spanning nearly 700 distinct locations in Beijing. Preliminary analysis indicated that verbal interactions often result in inconsistent information, reflecting the inherent nature of human communication. Furthermore, location references, which are critical for dispatching, frequently lack spatial context, posing another challenge. To resolve these issues, a proposed text mining system, named GeoCoder, can quickly determine locations mentioned in the calls and accurately infer relevant spatial information. An experimental evaluation of GeoCoder revealed promising results, with its performance surpassing that of several leading commercial spatial encoding methods. An in-depth case study was also conducted to demonstrate GeoCoder's effectiveness in enhancing the Beijing 119 dispatching system. An open-source version of GeoCoder, as well as the accompanying dataset, are available for public use. Future research can build upon GeoCoder, which can be further optimized to achieve even greater efficiency. Nonetheless, GeoCoder has already shown the capability to greatly improve the quality of location data, thus empowering other text-oriented community security systems worldwide. An in-depth discussion of potential research avenues is provided. In the end, GeoCoder has the potential to greatly advance the development of community security systems globally. We introduce a new framework, Minimax Engaged Learning, which addresses the issue of overfitting in machine learning models by implementing a competitive learning process between two players: a learner and a adversary. The game begins with the learner creating a model and the adversary evaluating its performance, while both players exchange essential information about the data. The learner's primary goal is to minimize the difference in assessment by adapting the model, while the adversary aims to maximize this difference by simulating the mentor's perspective. By engaging in this two-player game, the model is compelled to discover effective features that the teacher deems crucial, thereby preventing overfitting and enhancing the model's generalization capabilities according to the teacher's standards. We further investigate how the properties of the teacher influence the model and demonstrate its utility through experiments on regression, reinforcement learning, and 2-player game theory, revealing notable improvements in performance. The study also provides valuable insights into the characteristics of optimal teachers and learners under specific conditions. Lastly, a Minimax Engaged Learning library with essential tools is made available for public use. To study the time-dependent characteristics of music, we employed a sophisticated network approach based on eight detailed audio features extracted from popular songs over the past 50 years. Our analysis reveals significant shifts in music generated by temporary changes in song selection, rather than deliberate modifications to the underlying code of musical information. Between 1970 and 1990, music featured a mix of simple and complex elements, but the trend since 2000 has been increasingly sophisticated. Interestingly, the distribution of music samples becomes more concentrated over time, fitting a well-known statistical distribution more accurately in each decade. Our findings on music generated by automatic programs or neural networks suggest that these systems are capable of mimicking natural music evolution trends. By modeling music as an information stream with a constant data rate, we estimated the lifetime of modern music to be approximately 1,000 to 10,000 years under current conditions. Moreover, our research demonstrates the effectiveness of intricate feature analysis in capturing music evolution trends, which can provide a more accurate representation of music complexity than more basic representations. By publishing our code and using widely available music datasets, our study's replicability is ensured. This paper investigates the behavior of a reinforcement procedure with multiple entries, where a fixed number of experiments are conducted, each having a random duration governed by a Poisson distribution with a shared rate parameter. For each experiment, a tester accumulates rewards, denoted as a partial sum of a sequence of independent, identically distributed random variables. The tester stops exploring and stops recording rewards once a pre-determined total reward is reached. I examine how a sequence of these experiment termination values, properly scaled, behaves as the number of experiments grows. Specifically, I demonstrate that this behavior converges weakly to a Gamma-distribution. Additionally, I show that a related sequence of quantities, specifically the maximum of these experiment termination values, converges in probability to a quantity that can be represented as the maximum of a sequence of independent, identically distributed Gamma-distributed variables.
