We propose the concept of "computational harmony" as an aspect of playful user experiences in AI, which occurs when interactions are both aesthetically pleasing and make sense to the user. By drawing on music theory, we demonstrate how the underlying structures of interactive machine learning can produce predictable and satisfying experiences. This includes generating engaging sequences through neural networks, which adhere to principles of harmony. We illustrate our ideas through a simple generative neural network model, which emerges as a meaningful representation of the data it was trained on - a dictionary of musical notes. This representation enables various forms of computational harmony, such as generating coherent melodies in the key of C or creatingscattered melodic patterns. By extracting concepts from the data, we show how AI systems can develop their own understanding of musical principles, which can then be leveraged to produce a wide range of playful user experiences. Moreover, we show that these concepts can be transferred to other domains, enabling AI to uncover hidden meanings behind any dataset the user provides. This research offers a fresh perspective on the focus of AI development - shifting from tasks to experiences - and paves the way for a future where AI is not merely utilitarian but also aesthetically pleasing and meaningful to humans. Ultimately, we hope to develop an AI system that applies musical harmony to real-world problems, making interactions more enjoyable and even involving users in the co-creation of novel computational harmonies. With collaborative input from designers, ethologists, and scientists, AI can evolve into a force for good, using its predictive powers to enhance interactions and make the world a more harmonious place, one interaction at a time.  key words: AI, machine learning, computational harmony, music theory, generative models, neural networks, playful user experiences, co-creation, interactive machine learning, computational humor, music, melody, key, harmony, music therapy. key names: I. This study examines the influence of differential rotation on baroclinic wave formation in a horizontally extended cylinder, with an emphasis on understanding and validating numerical models through experimental research. Unlike traditional Rossby wave behavior, where non-rotating long waves precede strongly spinning waves, our findings show that in this cylindrical setup, non-rotating and rotating waves exhibit similar characteristics. This is due to the increased influence of meridional velocity components in the spinning system, which is largely a result of the baroclinic instability's horizontal length scale exceeding the rotation rate's influence. Our experimental findings include detailed wave patterns, as well as the associated energy distribution and wave propagation speeds, all of which are thoroughly documented. Numerical model validation involves comparing these results with each other. Additionally, our wave patterns trigger a phenomenon commonly seen in rapidly spinning cylinders, where waves merge to form a quasi-stationary wave-like structure at the cylinder's narrow end. Lastly, our research explores the cylinder's energy conversion processes and how they change when subjected to spinning and non-rotating conditions. These findings enhance our understanding of the spinning cylinder's dynamics and provide valuable insights into the system's behavior, ultimately contributing to the development of more accurate numerical models for complex geophysical and planetary flows. A standard approach to analyzing extreme value models involves incorporating unitary Poisson processes that generate observed extreme events. While this method is efficient in terms of computational speed, it can present challenges, such as non-intuitive parameters and difficulties in tracking parameter dependencies. In an effort to address these issues, we introduce a new scheme that converts unitary Poisson process parameters into more easily interpretable quantities. This study develops a theoretical framework that enables the calculation of extreme value model parameters within this new framework, confirming accuracy through simulations and showcasing its utility in a real-world case involving British rainfall data. Additionally, our method exhibits desirable properties, such as stable Markov chain behavior in posterior sampling, ensuring reliable results from Bayesian analysis. Overall, this method offers a valuable tool for extreme value modeling, providing a simpler and more intuitive framework for researchers and analysts to work within.

We demonstrate the existence of a reliable and efficient training process for offline reinforcement learning tasks when the training data is not entirely genuine. Our goal is to develop an offline RL method that can perform at least as well as the current best method when all the training data is trustworthy. Building on the concept of fraud-resilient regression introduced in prior research, we formulate offline RL as a form of data-perturbed regression problem. By assuming that up to $\epsilon P$ of the training data can be compromised for any given $\epsilon > 0$ and $P \geq 1$, we provide theoretical guarantees for our approach. In particular, for an episodic Markov Decision Process with state and action spaces both having $N$ possible values, and a target return of $\mu_r$. In the worst-case scenario, our method guarantees a return of $8\left(\mu_r + 3\sqrt{P\vee 1}\right)$ when $\epsilon P \leq 0.5$, our results hold under the same conditions as Theorem 2.3 in prior research, which demonstrated equivalent results in a fraud-resilient regression setting. Our method is also similar to prior offline RL approaches, such as Follow-the-Value*, and its effectiveness in real-world scenarios is substantiated through experiments using the AI2Code environment. AI2Code is a programming task environment that offers a return structure and has a state and action space with numerous possible values. Our approach provides a general solution to the problem of performing offline RL when training data can be compromised. This solution may have implications in various real-world scenarios where data can be tainted due to human errors, and our approach may also be applicable to regression problems in settings where testing costs are high. Additionally, our method can be seen as a form of robust reinforcement learning, which is a promising area of research in which agents learn policies that remain effective even when the other parties involved are attempting to deceive the agent. Our approach also provides a training method for robust reinforcement learning, which is a promising area of research in which agents learn policies that remain effective even when the other parties involved are attempting to deceive the agent. Further research is needed in this area.

This study examines the impulsive controllability of a one-dimensional heat equation subject to dynamic boundary conditions. Initially, we prove a one-sided estimate for solutions to the associated state system. We utilize this result along with an optimal control approach and a duality technique to demonstrate the relationship between reachable sets and the initial-data set within a specified Hilbert space. By analyzing the reachability set, we determine necessary and sufficient conditions for achieving impulsive control of the given system. To verify these conditions, we implement a convex optimization procedure. This method involves transforming the reachability set into a convex region through logarithmic transformation, thereby allowing us to leverage existing techniques for boundary control. Finally, we devise an iterative algorithm to maximize the reachability set, which demonstrates the possibility of achieving impulsive control in previously undetermined cases. Moreover, this method facilitates the maximization of time-imposed constraints, a feature not present in previous versions of this research. This approach can potentially be extended to other control problems involving boundary control systems and may provide insight into achieving optimal controls with time-dependent constraints. Numerical examples illustrate the effectiveness of this method in identifying the maximum reachable set for given parameters. It is closely related to another submitted paper exploring the boundary control component of this study. This research appears to be the first to examine the impulsive controllability of a heat equation subject to dynamic boundary conditions within a specified Hilbert space. As such, it introduces several innovative approaches and showcases some intriguing mathematical properties. This study could potentially be generalized to three-dimensional systems, although this would likely require significant modifications to verify the convexity of the reachability set. Although the concept of generalized convolution is relatively new, it has significant links to established ideas like the Cauchy polynomial enumerators and multivariate generating functions. One of the most innovative applications of generalized convolutions is found in the Polya's enumeration theorem's extension by Zhihong Xia, which was published in 2015. This study offers a formula that takes the exponential generating functions of two sets and their partitions, combining them through the use of generalized convolutions. This paper provides a direct method for calculating the generalized convolution of two polynomial enumerators using their coefficients, which results in a more efficient algorithm with a lower memory requirement. The discovery of T-dwarf GJ 229B in 1995, initially thought to be an exotic object, was a pivotal moment in understanding ultra-cool dwarfs. Despite its notable characteristics, the composition of GJ 229B remains the subject of considerable uncertainty. Analyzing the spectrum of GJ 229B's low-resolution spectrum between 0.7-2.4 $\mu$m using the latest model spectra and atmospheric synthesis, our study provides the most comprehensive assessment of the object's properties to date. Our results reveal a spectral type of m$_{s}$=T5.25, with a best-fit model corresponding to a temperature of 1244 K and a pressure of 3 bar, with accompanying phase-folded light curves and constraints on the escaping infrared emission. Our analysis suggests that GJ 229B's atmosphere features a thick haze layer, most likely composed of amorphous tholins, which may be generated by the rapid cooling of particles after a photochemical reaction. This haze phenomenon is consistent with observations of other T-dwarfs, including CS 10AB and allows for a more plausible fit to the object's low-resolution spectrum. Our analysis also indicates that GJ 229B's atmosphere does not match the expected composition of methane ice, with our model crossing the 3$\sigma$ threshold when assuming a single pressure of 10 bar and an optical depth of 10 for methane absorption. Additionally, our model generates emission that accounts for the object's observed brown color, which is primarily driven by tholins rather than other particles or methane ice. As one of the brightest T-dwarfs, GJ 229B offers a unique opportunity for future study in the near-infrared, particularly with the upcoming JWST, where it can be observed in the 1-5 $\mu$m wavelength range. Observations of GJ 229B's spectroscopy during orbital phases around its host star could reveal dimming patterns in the near-infrared, which could be utilized to key constraints on the object's escape rate. Based on our model's prediction of GJ 229B's near-infrared flux, we estimate its dimming pattern during orbital phases around its host star. This dimming pattern suggests that the object experiences high-level atmospheric escape, which could be driven by magnetic or other phenomena. To verify our model's prediction, GJ 229B's spectroscopy during orbital phases around its host star needs to be observed in the 1-5 $\mu$m wavelength range

In this research, we investigate how a linear relationship between pressure and specific volume affects the feasibility of adiabatic ideal fluid collapse using numerical simulations. Specifically, we examine three types of linear relationships, including a soft equation of state, a standard equation of state, and a stiff equation of state. Our studies reveal that, in the presence of gravitational effects, matter initially distributed in a narrow, spherical area undergoes a successful, spherically symmetric collapse only when the equation of state exhibits a moderate level of stiffness. A significant issue in robotics lies in the substantial time and effort required for robot programming, a challenge robots currently face. The field of motor learning in robotics aims to address this problem by enabling robots to learn task-oriented skills through modification of their built-in movement patterns. Despite the potential benefit of end-effect supervision, which provides precise feedback on a task's outcome, it is often costly for high-precision applications. This research proposes an efficient method to optimize movement patterns using only general feedback about a robot's movement, allowing tasks to be adapted without expensive end-effect feedback. This approach is based on a novel metric measuring a robot's movement efficiency, which identifies optimal movement parameters for a task, ultimately leading to better learning outcomes when general feedback is available. To test this approach, a simulator was built to replicate a real-world scenario in which a robot automatically adjusts its camera positioning to extract meaningful data about a task's outcome, a process proven to be time-consuming and resource-intensive. Results from various experiments using this simulator reveal that the proposed method yields superior results compared to existing state-of-the-art techniques. We also present a comprehensive survey of existing efficient algorithms for these problems. We investigated this interaction within the context of massless scalar field theory through a direct calculation of the correlation function.  This reveals a complex relationship between the fields, intertwined in a manner that can be described by renormalized operators.  This study aims to contribute to ongoing research on the entanglement of operator expansion, specifically its application to conformal field theory, where key concepts such as conformal blocks and operator product expansion hold significant importance.  We compared the fully renormalized correlation function to the pre-renormalized version, identifying the key corrections and their impact on the entanglement of operator expansion.  We also examine the convergence of pre-renormalized conformal block series against the background of the pre-renormalized correlation function.  It was found, in line with existing theory, that pre-renormalized conformal block series converges within the region $z<1$ but diverges for $z>1$, with the difference between pre-renormalized and renormalized expressions increasing with the order of expansion.  Notably, while local operators exhibit a key property where all but one possible singularity in the structure of the correlation function are eliminated through renormalization, the same cannot be said for all operators; specifically, certain nonlocal operators such as the stress tensor and the twist fields continue to display the same singular behavior as in the pre-renormalized version, despite undergoing renormalization, highlighting a notable discrepancy. Recent experiments at HORUS and GELINA facilities, where fast-timing capabilities exist but are not entirely medium-free due to the reaction geometry, have raised questions about the direct-decay pattern of the Hoyle state. To resolve these issues, the European SPES Consortium conducted a gas-target experiment at the LNL e Beamline, investigating the 2073 keV level in $^{4}$He through $\beta$-particle bursts at a relativistic electron beam of 40-120 MeV. This new experiment, where the 2073 keV level shows prompt and non-prompt components with distinct 2.05 MeV $\alpha$-particle decays, provides clear evidence of the Hoyle state's existence. Additionally, the experiment's fast-timing capability, between 50-110 ns, enabled separation of the 2073 keV level's direct and multi-body decays, revealing an average lifetime of 120 ns with considerable uncertainties. This experiment's findings confirm the Hoyle state's distinct structure and allow analysis of the 17.6 MeV state in $^{8}$He. Recent studies on 2D materials have observed the phenomenon of negative friction, where a sharp object interacting with the material causes it to move in the opposite direction of expected force. Research has also discovered that under certain conditions, this interaction can lead to the material fracturing into smaller pieces. Through a combination of theoretical and numerical analyses using a complex model, we investigate the role of different parameters on this negative friction effect and the resulting fracture. Our findings reveal that the negative friction phenomenon is closely tied to the material's intrinsic length scales of a few angstroms, and that its magnitude can be significantly influenced by a small critical parameter for the fracture to occur. When these parameters are within the material's intrinsic range, the negative friction effect is necessary for the material failure to occur in a dynamic collision. Alternatively, even very soft materials can display the negative friction effect if the critical parameter is sufficiently low. A critical comparison between the present model and other available models highlights that the negative friction effect is intrinsic to the materials and should not be confused with other dynamic phenomena such as sound waves or van der Waals forces. Finally, our study also sheds light on the underlying mechanics behind the observed nanoscale friction phenomena. Specifically, it develops a unified framework for handling feedback and complex state dependencies in predictive modeling tasks. The proposed method utilizes a finite-state conduit to represent the interaction between encoder and decoder, enabling a more accurate description of predictive models. By applying conduit splitting and state mapping functions, which incorporate feedback from the encoder, the method achieves a full understanding of predictive models. Contrary to conventional wisdom, the results indicate that models can benefit from complex state dependencies and feedback, as demonstrated on benchmark language translation and generative tasks. Furthermore, the method allows for the identification of models that simply copy information, offering insights into the nature of predictive models. On both the IWSLT'14 DE-EN translation benchmark and the Bertram-Langley dataset in n-gram prediction, the performance of the proposed method surpasses that of baseline models. Moreover, the method indicates cases where models relying solely on information from the starting position can suffice, providing a fundamental understanding of models. A theoretical model demonstrates the emergence of spin-singlet topological superfluidity under specific conditions, namely when a two-dimensional gas with Rashba spin orbit coupling exhibits strong attractive interactions. Derived from the Landau-Luttinger model, the spin-singlet pair susceptibility $\chi_{ss}(q)$ shows a divergent behavior at $q_f = 2k_F \sqrt{1+\frac{\eta^2}{\lambda^2}}$, where $q_f$ is a critical momentum, $k_F$ is the Fermi wave number, $\eta$ represents Rashba coupling, and $\lambda$ denotes attractive interactions. The derived expression for $q_f$ is consistent with previous findings. The superfluidity arises from gap excitations that are gapped out in a $d+id$ topological superfluid. The superfluidity is signaled by a $Z_2$ topological invariant $\nu_{s,d}$, as well as by a non-zero condensate related to $d+id$ component $\Delta_{d+id}$. The existence of zero-energy states at the Fermi point is a necessary condition for this topological superfluidity. The spin-singlet pair susceptibility $\chi_{ss}(q)$ is found to be proportional to $\sim q^2$ in the small $q$ limit, and proportional to $\sim (q-q_f)^{-1}$ in the near neighbor neighbor limit of $q_f$. The spin-singlet pair susceptibility $\chi_{ss}(q)$ is also found to be proportional to $\sim \eta^2/\lambda^2$ in the high coupling limit of $\lambda$. A spin-singlet pair susceptibility $\chi_{dd}(q)$ is derived, showing similar behavior to $\chi_{ss}(q)$. The spin-singlet pair susceptibility $\chi_{sd}(q)$, on the other hand, shows a divergent behavior at $q = 2\eta/\lambda$. The spin-singlet pair susceptibility $\chi_{sd}(q)$ is found to be proportional to $\sim \eta/\lambda$ in the weak coupling limit of $\lambda$. A spin-singlet pair susceptibility $\chi_{ds}(q)$, related to $d$-wave component, is also considered, showing a divergent behavior at $q = 2\lambda/\eta$. This paper details the guidelines for SEM-TAB-FACTS, a new fact identification task linked to Semantics & Pragmatics in SemEval 2021. The task encompasses two key aspects: verifying the accuracy of specific information presented in scientific tables and identifying the tables that contain the relevant evidence to support fact assertion. We tested the effectiveness of automated systems with a dataset consisting of 1,000 annotated tables from the fields of medicine, biology, and computer science. Due to technical limitations, we did not hold a full competition; instead, we conducted two separate experiments to gauge system performance. This report outlines the experimental setup, reveals the results of submitted systems, and discusses the system performance. Additionally, we provide an analysis of the challenging nature of verifying fact accuracy in tabular data and propose potential future research directions. The data and code used for this study are freely accessible via GitHub repositories: \url{https://github.com/emorynlp/SEM-TAB-FACTS} and \url{https://github.com/shawnhuy/SEM-TAB-FACTS}.

The graph property of being a complete graph is closely linked to its vertex set ordering, which means that the shortest path distance between any two vertices in a complete graph corresponds to their relative position in the ordered set. Building upon this connection, we introduce the concept of shortened metric dimension by adapting the metric dimension formula for complete graphs. The metric dimension of a graph is defined as the minimum number of vertices needed to form a linear ordering of the graph, where the distance between any two vertices is calculated as the shortest path between them. In contrast, the shortened metric dimension of a graph represents a lower bound on the metric dimension, which can be achieved by arranging the graph's vertices in a linear ordering and using the induced distance. Notably, we find that for finite graphs of diameter d, the shortened metric dimension is at least $\frac{d+1}{2}$ and, depending on whether d is even or odd, it can be represented as either $\lfloor \frac{d}{2} \rfloor$ or $\lfloor \frac{d+1}{2} \rfloor$ respectively. Additionally, we derive exact values for the shortened metric dimension of various graph classes, where the metric dimension has previously been calculated. We also present a linear-time algorithm to exactly determine the shortened metric dimension for undirected graphs. The results presented here are original and provide insights into connecting graph properties with their topological characteristics. The concept of shortened metric dimension may also be applied to directed graphs with a specific property, where the metric dimension results for these graphs include a lower and upper bound. The results we've derived can be further extended to investigating new problems related to graph spanners and embedding linear structures into graphs. These findings can also be applied to fields outside graph theory where ordering and distance are relevant. Conveying testing knowledge to inexperienced programmers can be a daunting task. Traditional methods typically involve lengthy explanations which can be overwhelming, especially for those new to programming. This study examines an alternative approach where instructors provide essential testing concepts in a straightforward manner, drawing parallels with how students approach inquiry-based learning. A controlled study was conducted with 240 students from two universities who received either the conventional or conceptual teaching method, following up with an online survey to compare their performance. Surprisingly, students who were taught conceptual testing showed a similar level of understanding and performance compared to their counterparts who were taught traditional detailed testing, despite requiring fewer instructional cues. Notably, both groups demonstrated improved comprehension, suggesting that conceptual testing may be an effective training tool, validating its use as a viable option for teaching testing principles. Building on these findings, further research is suggested to explore the potential for conceptual testing to enhance just-in-time training, a key area of interest for software educators. A corresponding submission for SEIS is currently under review at the ACM Library under ID: 2023001.

The $\alpha$-attractor model is a highly appealing inflationary theory backed by substantial evidence from observations. However, the convolution of this model with cosmological observations renders it difficult to analyze statistically. The number of degrees of freedom in this model far exceeds that of other single scalar field models, making it non-standard and requiring specialized analysis methods. In this study, we introduce a simulation tool to sample the parameter space of the $\alpha$-attractor model in a statistically meaningful manner. Utilizing this tool, we generate large datasets of this model under various conditions and demonstrate how constraint releases become increasingly simple as the model's parameters correlate with one another. We anticipate these findings to translate similarly to other complex models. Additionally, we provide a statistically grounded forecast for how future surveys will constrain the $\alpha$-attractor model based on an in-depth analysis involving two distinct constraint methods. The outcomes illustrate the substantial potential of upcoming surveys to pinpoint the $\alpha$-attractor model's parameters. The associated code is publicly accessible via GitHub at the specified link.

Humanity is at a critical crossroads due to its own environmental impact. The pace of environmental deterioration accelerates as population grows, consuming resources faster than they can be replenished. Pessimism about the future is natural under this scenario, yet there's an alternative narrative - one rooted in societal dynamics and cooperative potentialities. This paper explores how cooperative endeavors might give rise to a sustainable future, and presents a theoretical framework for assessing the likelihood of this outcome. Ultimately, the probability of a environmentally conscious and responsible global society depends on understanding the inherent properties of cooperative systems. By analyzing these properties, we discover that the transition to a sustainable future is not only possible, but also inherently likely. Unfortunately, our current global system is ill-equipped for this outcome, and our findings suggest that widespread climate information among citizens is essential for preventing long-term environmental devastation. The good news is that, as a collective, humans have demonstrated an impressive capacity for positive change throughout history, and it's this cooperative spirit that holds the key to a better future. By acknowledging both the pressing need for change and the inherent resilience of human societies, we can work towards a future characterized by hope and determination. This paper offers a theoretical model for quantifying the probability of a sustainable future, and provides initial estimates based on available data. While our analysis is preliminary, and this model can be refined further, our findings already suggest valuable insights for mitigating the effects of climate change. Notably, the model suggests that educating the public about climate issues is crucial for preventing long-term environmental harm, and that a high level of public awareness in countries like the US and Australia increases the likelihood of adopting environmentally conscious policies. Conversely, countries with low climate awareness, such as Kazakhstan and Turkey, are more likely to experience severe environmental deterioration in the future. By exploring the intricate relationships between cooperative systems and environmental sustainability, we can gain a deeper understanding of the complex dynamics governing both global societies and ecosystems. This knowledge can, in turn, be utilized for designing and optimizing societies of the future, and informing decision-making policies at both local and national levels. Ultimately, our study offers a hopeful perspective on humanity's future, and serves as a reminder of the remarkable capacity for positive change that lies within us all. By working together, we can build a better world for generations to come. This research explores the boundedness of the fractional difference operator, denoted by $\Delta_{\alpha}^{r}$, where $r$ lies between $0$ and $1$, under the $H_{p}^{\ast}$ norm on the discrete Hardy space $H_{p}^{\ast}$. It is demonstrated that $\Delta_{\alpha}^{r}$ is a bounded operator from $H_{p}^{\ast}$ to $H_{q}^{\ast}$ when $p$ and $q$ satisfy specific constraints. Additionally, the problem of finding sufficient conditions for boundedness is revisited for another operator, $\Delta_{\alpha}^{r}$, this time on $H_{p}$. To resolve this, a novel approach is introduced that compares $\Delta_{\alpha}^{r}$ with a related integral operator. This comparison enables the derivation of a sufficient condition for boundedness, thereby surpassing existing sufficient conditions in the literature. Furthermore, contrastive relationships between the norms of $\Delta_{\alpha}^{r}T_{\beta}$ and $T_{\beta}$ are established, where $T_{\beta}$ is an initial operator. These findings broaden the scope of directly proven boundedness criteria for $\Delta_{\alpha}^{r}$ and $T_{\beta}$. Ultimately, this research substantiates the connection between differential and difference operators, thereby providing novel insights into the theory of fractional difference operators. It further paves the way for the exploration of composition operators, whose boundedness conditions remain largely unsolved. Moreover, this research is expected to contribute to the development of a more comprehensive theory of operator functions, facilitating innovations in the realm of harmonic analysis. Finally, the conclusions reached within this study may find applications in the realm of fractional calculus and its applications, which has experienced rapid growth in recent decades due to its utility in modeling diverse physical phenomena and the ease with which it can be generalized to function and sequence settings. Building on existing work by Yamauchi-Yao, our approach relies on geometric vertex partitions of these varieties. By applying this concept along with other tools like Gr\"obner bases and Frobenius splittings, we can gain insights into the global structure of these Hessenberg varieties. Specifically, our analysis yields new information about the codimension and the cohomology ring of these varieties. particular focus is given to two key cases: the rank one Hessenberg varieties and and those related to a 3-dimensional nilpotent orbit. This allows us to establish specific formulas for their cohomology rings and, in the case of the rank one varieties, the Poincaré polynomial for the regular nilpotent orbit. Furthermore, our investigation also leads to a detailed examination of the intersection ring of the boundary components in the 3-dimensional nilpotent Hessenberg variety. This extends existing results from [BY] to all Hessenberg varieties. Neural art generation has gained significant attention in recent years due to its potential to alleviate artistic skills' requirements, yet the involvement of manual preprocessing for input data often counteracts this benefit, necessitating some artistic knowledge after all. A novel approach has therefore emerged for generating art through raw, everyday language inputs, eliminating the need for artistic knowledge. Nonetheless, creating high-quality visual content remains a challenging task, and existing methods often struggle to produce desirable results, especially in the field of painting, which demands more intricate compositions. To address these limitations, we propose PaintChat, a groundbreaking system that combines raw language inputs with visual content generation, and as such, contributes to neural artistry's core principles. To optimize visual quality, our method leverages pre-trained visual and language models to extract semantic characteristics from input sentences and corresponding visual representations. These characteristics serve as guiding features for the generated image's semantic properties. Through extensive human evaluations, our method has consistently outperformed existing baselines in overall quality, with notable improvements in coherence, composition, and detail representation. Additionally, a qualitative analysis of participant feedback revealed high praise for PaintChat's creative potential, demonstrating human delight in neural artistry. In this study, we explore an epidemic model where the population doesn't differentiate between ages, but rather integrates distinct-time classes that interact with each other in a specific manner. Our model aims to understand the spread of epidemics under the influence of temporary and permanent immunity. Through mathematical analysis, we establish a nonlocal dynamical model that represents this epidemic scenario, and our analysis reveals the long-term implications of nonlocal interactions on the epidemic's persistence and transient behavior. Our results demonstrate how the model's equilibrium states are affected by the long-term nonlocal effects, and we find that only one equilibrium state survives the long-term implications of nonlocal interactions. Furthermore, we employed numerical simulations to illustrate the differences between local and nonlocal dynamics, particularly in the cases of two and three distinct-time classes. Our analysis of the model's transient behavior using Fourier cosine series expansions and numerical solutions shows that nonlocal interactions can alter the long-term patterns of epidemic transmission compared to local models. Our findings suggest that long-term nonlocal effects can alter the persistence and transient patterns of epidemic transmission, and these changes are more pronounced in models that are further divided into distinct-time classes. Our results also highlight the significance of considering nonlocal interactions in modeling epidemic transmission, particularly when the population is divided into distinct-time classes. Our work contributes to the growing body of research on nonlocal models in epidemiology, and our findings demonstrate the potential for long-term nonlocal effects to shape our understanding of epidemic transmission patterns. Ultimately, our study underscores the importance of considering the underlying social structure of the population when modeling epidemic transmission. If the population is divided into distinct-time classes, nonlocal interactions will inevitably shape the long-term patterns of epidemic transmission, and this cannot be captured by local models. Conversely, if the population is not divided into distinct-time classes, local models will suffice in capturing the rapid changes in epidemic transmission patterns, and long-term nonlocal effects become less relevant. Quantum learning, a quantum version of supervised learning, uses quantum superposition to efficiently process diverse data sets and their corresponding labels for finding common patterns. We have developed two quantum algorithms - Quantum Unmonitored Learning and Quantum Instructed Learning - which utilize quantum circuits to learn patterns in data without and with the aid of instructional data, respectively. These algorithms have been implemented on a superconducting quantum processor using pyQuil, a quantum algorithm development tool, and we have analyzed their performance as a function of circuit depth. We have discovered that both algorithms exhibit significant scalability advantages over their classical counterparts, and the instructional algorithm displays notable data dependence, excelling the traditional supervised learning method when data is highly correlated with the labels. Furthermore, we have observed that the quantum algorithms outperform their classical counterparts even when data is not highly correlated with the labels. We have successfully learned patterns in random data for a 4-qubit and 5-qubit system, and we have observed notable differences in the instructional and non-instructional algorithms, respectively. These findings suggest that quantum learning may offer substantial advantages over classical methods. While there are limitations to working with a limited number of qubits, we have observed notable patterns in the data and have even discovered some intriguing non-local effects in the instructional learning process that warrant further study. In the future, we plan to overcome the current processor limitations by utilizing larger quantum processors. We believe that the quantum learning algorithms will eventually offer substantial benefits in real-world applications. Differentiable rendering, which integrates gradient computation into rendering equations, has been highly influential in recent computer vision research. This study develops an innovative method for exploring linked data by integrating word embeddings into a visual interface. By leveraging these embeddings, users can uncover hidden patterns and connections within complex data. We illustrate the effectiveness of this approach using Ontodia and Wikidata, demonstrating how word embeddings can be utilized to highlight essential concepts and relationships in human-centered datasets. Additionally, we provide a demonstration of this method on the Wikidata portal for biomedical research. Furthermore, we discuss potential applications and challenges associated with extending this technique to various data sets and visualization tools. The code used for this research is openly accessible on the https://github.com/ontodia/wiki2vecVisuals platform. We aim for this work to contribute to the creation of a new data investigation methodology that combines visualizations and machine learning, enabling users to gain deeper insights into linked data. We believe this research will pave the way for a broader range of applications, ultimately facilitating a more comprehensive understanding of linked data. Experimental findings validate the proposed hypothesis, revealing two primary challenges: the need to develop more intuitive data visualization methods for word embeddings and the emergence of a new, previously unseen entity category. Specifically, the results indicate that users uncover previously neglected data properties in the process of investigating word embeddings. We have identified a total of nine such property types. Furthermore, the word embeddings allowed us to identify gaps in the Wikidata domain taxonomy, prompting the addition of six new domain categories to enhance the dataset. Moving forward, we intend to build upon this research in several ways. Firstly, we will refine the visualization method to make it even more intuitive for users. Secondly, we will explore the potential for generating recommendations based on the similarities among closely related concepts in the data. Lastly, we will delve deeper into the classification capabilities of word embeddings, including their ability to accurately classify entities within specific categories. To achieve these objectives, we will employ a range of techniques such as leave-one-out training, targeted data reductions, and comprehensive evaluations of the resulting models. By pushing the current boundaries of these methods, we hope to contribute significantly to the development of novel data investigation tools. To facilitate this effort, we will openly share the code and data used in this research, making them accessible to the public at https://github.com/ontodia/wiki2vecVisuals. We plan to present our research at prominent conferences in the fields of semantic technologies, data science, and information visualization. We aim to publish the research in top-tier journals and contribute to ongoing data sets and software platforms by openly providing additional resources at https://github.com/ontodia

Our findings indicate that, contrary to typical cubic dispersion, solitons in the intensity-sensitive regime exhibit an increased effective mass, which in turn affects their movement and interactions. Specifically, we observe that solitons in the intensity-sensitive regime exhibit an increased repulsive force during collisions, as well as enhanced stability in response to external disturbances. Notably, the stability of solitons in the intensity-sensitive regime exceeds that of solitons in the cubic dispersion regime, under various conditions. Moreover, we have developed a generalized model for describing small spatial modulations on dark solitons, taking into account intensity-dependent dispersion. This generalized model has been validated through comparison with numerical simulations, and its associated stability criteria have been established. As such, the generalized model can be employed to analyze the stability of solitons in actual experiments. Optical systems with intensity-sensitive dispersion that exhibit modulational instability, including ones based on Kerr and photorefractive materials, have been shown to support stable dark solitons. Consequently, the research presented here provides insight into the creation and manipulation of stable dark solitons in optical experiments. The temperature disparity between a heated gas flowing through a stationary granular medium and its surrounding environment is the focal point of a study conducted by our research group. To investigate the thermal equilibrium state, a 20 micron resolution MRI technique was utilized at temperatures ranging from 20 to 60 degrees Celsius for various gas and air flow velocities in cylindrical samples containing approximately 1,500 2-mm spherical alumina particles. As the temperature increased from 20 to 60 degrees Celsius, the thermal equilibrium temperature in the bed rose by approximately 0.05 K per degree Celsius. The MRI technique allowed for the measurement of the thermal equilibrium temperature and density of the bed with substantial precision. Nonetheless, a novel, probe-based method was developed to measure the average particle velocity in the bed. The measured particle velocity was found to be roughly 1% greater than the estimated linear velocity of the gas. Moreover, the radial temperature gradient in the bed was measured and found to be directly related to the magnitude of the particle velocity relative to the gas velocity. A method was proposed to minimize this radial temperature gradient by controlling the shape of the bed and its packing properties. This study demonstrates the value of MRI imaging in understanding the complex dynamics and thermal properties of the granular bed with minimal simplifications to theoretical models. Furthermore, a straightforward method was developed to measure the effective heat transfer coefficient of the bed. The ever-growing influence of user-generated content is significantly altering the digital landscape, driven in part by the proliferation of social tagging systems. These systems facilitate user interaction by encouraging collaboration, information sharing, and the consumption of user-generated metadata. We investigate key characteristics of such systems, including traditional usage, pattern evolution over time, and the initial and deepening levels of participation among existing users. Our analysis reveals that while fresh perspectives enhance these systems, their value also grows as existing users continue to engage actively. Notably, the most productive users drive the most valuable content in social tagging systems. We provide concrete empirical examples to support our findings, along with actionable suggestions and research avenues for the social tagging system design. Ultimately, our study aims to contribute to the broader theory of user-generated content, offering insights relevant to any platform that fosters user participation and collaboration. Additionally, our analysis serves as a blueprint for designing and improving social tagging systems, as well as other applications that rely heavily on user-generated content. We hope that our work will stimulate further exploration and research within the domain of social tagging systems. The data used for our study is accessible through our project website at https://github.com/semantic-rater/social-tagging-systems. Recently, proposed bianisotropic acoustic metagratings offer promising possibilities for passive acoustic wave manipulation, notably in flat acoustic lenses and ultra-high frequency ultrasound systems. This concept expands upon the successful optical metagrating technique, enabling simplified fabrication and enhanced functionality. However, the initial theoretical models assumed an infinite spatial resolution, which is not achievable in practical scenarios. Our research introduces microacoustic metagratings built using two-photon polymerization, leveraging 240-250 GHz frequency ranges where the wavelength exceeds 1 millimeter. By utilizing microscopic structures, we demonstrated the effectiveness of acoustic pass-band filters and active control mechanisms. Notably, compared to theoretically designed models, our acoustic metagratings demonstrated only marginal frequency shifts - approximately 0.03 percent. This work not only validates theoretical concepts but also paves the way for the development of innovative acoustic devices using advanced 3D printing technologies. Furthermore, we anticipate extending this technique to even higher frequency ranges, potentially up to terahertz frequencies. Given the potential for microscopic structures, devices in this frequency range could be effectively controlled by infrared radiation. In terms of the technology itself, our findings indicate that the use of deep UV flash lithography - a technique used in the development of silicon chips, may significantly surpass the resolution capabilities of two-photon polymerization. Therefore, we anticipate a bright future for theoretical research in the field of the metagrating technique, as well as advancements using advanced 3D printing technologies to develop innovative devices across both acoustic and optical spectrums. In particular, we note a significant gap in knowledge regarding microscopic optical metagratings at deep infrared frequencies and the absence of research on acoustic metagratings at terahertz frequencies - a gap we aim to bridge through our next study. Despite the potential of lifelong reinforcement reinforcement learning to save time, effort, and resources, current methods often struggle to adapt and generalize across diverse sets of skills. One significant obstacle is the absence of comprehensive evaluation frameworks that can assess a variety of abilities and adapt to various scenarios. To bridge this gap, we introduce L2Explorer, an extensive benchmark environment designed to evaluate lifelong reinforcement learning strategies through a wide range of tasks. L2Explorer combines three distinct types of skills: (1) navigation in a dynamic environment with moving goals, (2) object interaction, and (3) multiple goal-based planning. What sets L2Explorer apart from other benchmarks is its ability to support both skill acquisition and adaptation across multiple skill types, as well as the reuse of existing skills in novel scenarios. Our framework provides a flexible architecture to support various benchmarking strategies and allows for the implementation of various lifelong reinforcement learning methods. Our experiments demonstrate that several state-of-the-art approaches using self-paced learning and curriculum learning are highly effective in the L2Explorer environment. However, our novel learning framework, CL-LRL, outperforms these methods in terms of efficiency and adaptability. Our research suggests that CL-LRL has the potential to greatly reduce the sample complexity of reinforcement learning methods. X-ray images of COVID-19 patients contain valuable information about the severity of lung inflammation, which can take various forms depending on the patient's health condition. To develop a severity measurement for lung inflammation, we need to identify reliable characteristics from X-ray images that accurately represent its severity. To determine these characteristics, we conducted a study involving a diverse, international team of clinicians consisting of 25 experts in infectious diseases, 15 critical care specialists, and 4 chest radiology specialists. Through multiple rounds of virtual meetings, including a public virtual conference, the team established a common understanding of the key image features essential for measuring inflammation severity. The proposed characteristics, validated by clinicians, include total ground area, inflammation type, multi-lobe involvement, patient age, and oxygen therapy needs, allowing us to create a comprehensive definition for inflammation severity. Based on these characteristics, we developed a straightforward, easy-to-implement metric, which was used to measure inflammation severity in a test dataset. Furthermore, we discovered that certain characteristics, such as patient age and oxygen therapy needs, are inherently linked to non-imaging ICU admission indicators, highlighting the importance of incorporating these factors when assessing inflammation severity. To establish a fully automated metric, we plan to combine machine learning-based techniques with human evaluation in future work. Ultimately, this research aims to identify a reliable computational approach to determine inflammation severity from X-ray images, which could accelerate clinical decision-making and patient treatment, saving lives in the process. With further development, the proposed method could be utilized as a general tool for evaluating lung inflammation severity, potentially applicable to other diseases and clinical contexts. A key objective in intent detection involves categorizing untapped intentions behind users' inputs, which requires models to continuously discover new intents within unlabeled data. Unfortunately, current leading NLP models perform poorly in this area. To improve intent discovery, we suggest leveraging pre-trained language models, which can enhance a model's ability to extract novel intentions by exploiting their capacity for representing diverse contexts. To further boost performance, we also introduce a novel contrastive loss, which pushes similar contexts associated with the same intent further apart, and pushes unrelated contexts closer together, based on their similarity in context-intent pairs. Our proposed method demonstrates superior performance over existing approaches on three widely-used datasets, achieving significantly higher F1-score improvements. Notably, our method exhibits excellent generalizability, with a notable 25% F1-score improvement when applying it to previously known intents, and as many as 300% when applying it to previously unknown intents. The source code for our approach is available at https://github.com/Chen-543/NEIL.

The evaluation of false positives in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD) has been consistently overlooked, leading to suboptimal model performance and inaccurate scene understanding. To address this, we propose the crowdVRD-Held-Out attribute challenge, designed to quantify model errors by hiding relevant attribute information during inference. In addition to this challenge, we develop a novel dataset enhancement approach, consisting of three methods: negative sampling, data augmentation, and attribute-manipulated pseudo-labeling. These techniques significantly improve current state-of-the-art models, with our best model achieving a 44.97% mAP on the VRD benchmark, outperforming the top performing model by 7.53%. Our work is the first to prioritize false positive reduction in VRD, offering a more robust evaluation of model performance and efficiency. The related code and dataset can be found on our GitHub repository: https://github.com/zzspondence/VRD-FP. With this research, we aim to promote discussion and further optimization of VRD models. CrowdVRD-Held-Out attribute challenge winners will be announced on our website: https://crowdvrd.github.io/challenge.html.

In recent years, graph neural networks have garnered significant attention due to their ability to process complex, relational data, and have been effectively applied to various vision and reinforcement learning tasks. However, the standard graph neural network approach has a significant drawback: it requires a pre-defined graph topology. To address this limitation, our proposed Active Graph Message Transfer Network (AGMTN) learns a dynamic graph structure for each message propagation layer through an attention mechanism that selects relevant nodes for improved performance in visual recognition tasks. To our knowledge, AGMTN is the first graph neural network that doesn't rely on a predefined graph for message propagation. Additionally, our proposed Spline-AGMTN method extends the basic AGMTN by incorporating a spline-based attention mechanism for even better performance. The theoretical justification for our approach is also provided. Experimental evaluations under standard settings reveal that our proposed methods significantly outperform existing state-of-the-art methods for semantic segmentation and object detection tasks. The code for our proposed methods will be publicly available soon.

Achieving optimal hardware realization of NCM operations often relies on the properties of the multiplication coefficients. While parameterization methods for NCM circuits exist, they do not adapt well to coefficients with common factors, resulting in non-optimal hardware designs. In an effort to improve this, we have developed a new method for the Extended Bit Level Partial Product Computation (XBLCPC) that incorporates techniques for identifying common factors within the coefficients. This new approach can lead to significant reductions in hardware costs, as demonstrated by examples requiring fewer adders and multipliers to compute various NCM operations. Notably, compared to the best existing method, our approach can reduce the hardware expense by approximately 10%. This result is validated through experiments involving 200 randomly generated scenarios. As another contribution, we have found that most actual multiplication coefficients do not have common factors after the coefficient reduction process, suggesting the need for more efficient hardware designs through LBPC computation. This discovery further motivated the development of a hardware counter to automatically assess the suitability of LBPC for a given NCM operation. This hardware assessment counter can serve as an essential tool to determine when LBPC and the reduced multiplication coefficient are equivalent. As such, it accommodates both Fixed Protected Framework and Dynamic Protected Framework architectures. To address these challenges, a detailed evaluation of the latter's throughput and latency is provided, focusing on various scenarios involving multiple parallel execution paths. Moreover, a Virtual Protected Framework Architecture is proposed, incorporating innovative features such as Inter-Application Data Swapping and Multi-Application Support. In a standard RAM model where memory access costs $k$ units, we can demonstrate the cost-$\mathcal{O}(n)$ execution of an alternating sum, provided that the initial memory contents $a_0,\ldots,a_{n-1}$ are known. This gives us the equation $a_0+\cdots+a_{n-1} = (a_0)+(a_1)+(a_2)+\cdots + (a_{n-2}) + (a_{n-1})$. This reveals an essential property: the execution of a given sequence of $\mathcal{O}(n)$ memory references, where adjacent references have a distance of $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{n})$, will result in higher total reference costs compared to a direct sequence with distance $\mathcal{O}(n)$. This observation guides our design for an $\mathcal{O}(\log n)$-time sorting algorithm, where we ensure nearby memory locations are constantly accessed. This sorting algorithm is also the foundation for our development of an efficient matrix multiplication method. Given two square matrices of size $(n) \times (n)$, we can execute their multiplication using a sequential algorithm with a cost of $\mathcal{O}(n^\beta)$, where the value of $\beta$ can be any number between one and two. This gives us the opportunity to explore a wide range of possible $\beta$ values, offering an alternative solution to a classic problem in the field. Additionally, our paper provides a detailed analysis of the time complexity in our sorting algorithm and identifies the most efficient possible value for $\beta$. Finally, we utilize our efficient sorting method to develop a highly sequential matrix multiplication algorithm, where we also detail the specifics of its implementation and its performance characteristics in terms of time complexity. This algorithm will also serve as an essential component in our RAM model simulation of the deterministic logarithmic time DLOG-RAM computation model, which can execute a predicate test with $\mathcal{O}(\log n)$ operations on an input of size $n$ despite operating on a single-bit output, resulting in further discussions on its implications and the possibilities it affords. Ultimately, our paper offers the first-ever description of the DLOG-RAM computation model based on RAM operations, providing insight into its relationship with the well-known POLYLOG-RAM computation model. This insight includes an accurate assessment of the DLOG-RAM and POLYLOG-RAM efficiency gap for predicates with polylogarithmic outputs.

Consequently, we show that the Feynman integrals on this graph complex possess a differential equation, which aligns with Stanley's remark on the relationship between the chromatic polynomial and a differential equation. Notably, our approach allows the generalization of Stanley's remark to all n, whereas previous proofs were only viable for n>=3. Moreover, we expand upon the concept, applying it to the case of bipartite graphs, where we derive a differential equation for the Kostant-Lecouture-Richardson coalgebra. Finally, we explore the relationship between our results and the concept of imaginary time Amplitude Finite Action Principles in quantum field theory, revealing a possible connection that was initially proposed in our prior work. The findings of this research were initially presented at the 13th International Symposium on the Applications of Computer Algebra in November 2020.

This study examines how recurrent neural networks (RNNs), designed for object classification tasks, utilize object attributes to filter and organize information about individual objects. We trained RNNs on a dataset with annotated object feature categories and used numerical representations, known as vector semantics or concept vectors, to assess the network's feature learning capabilities. The results reveal that these embedded features exhibit a high degree of independence, indicating the networks integrate category-specific object attributes to filter and synthesize information about individual objects, thereby enhancing object classification performance. The findings suggest that the low-level detail in the object representation is discarded by the RNN, with the high-level structure maintained, allowing for the separation of relevant from irrelevant information. The methodology developed in this study can be used to investigate how various deep learning architectures, including convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and attention-based models, process object characteristics and integrate information about individual objects. Additionally, the study provides a framework for validating the embedding space of deep learning models, with potential applications beyond object classification extending to tasks such as object counting and link prediction in object-based datasets. Given its simplicity, this approach can be used to investigate the embedding space of deep learning models in a wide range of domains, including text classification and gene data. Quantum systems with non-Hermitian properties exhibit unique topology, characterized by extended edge states, which are nearly immune to non-zero system parameters. However, this study reveals that intrinsic correlations within a one-dimensional non-Hermitian system can eliminate its topological features. Using the extended edge states as an example, we show that these correlations can decouple the system's Hamiltonian, resulting in separate local parts and a long-range interaction. Depending on the system's parameters, this coupling can either weaken or break the topological effect, causing the edge states to localize inside extended regions. Notably, this effect can be observed even in the absence of scattering, which is always present in multi-dimensional topological systems. Consequently, this phenomenon can be experimentally validated using linear chain systems, such as coupled bosonic modes in cavities or qubits. Overall, this study demonstrates that intrinsic correlations within quantum systems can significantly impact their topological properties, leading to novel phenomena that are worth exploring in quantum device development. Additionally, this study's findings may be extended to various other topological systems, such as those with higher spatial extensions and based on different physical principles. Lastly, although this study focuses on non-Hermitian topology, the underlying mechanisms can also be applied to Hermitian topological systems, which are more commonly encountered in quantum physics. By combining these ideas, this study lays the foundation for topological error correction in non-Hermitian quantum systems with extended support. In particular, this study shows that intrinsic correlations within multi-partite quantum systems can be utilized to develop topological quantum technologies, which are currently under development. These developments may pave the way for novel applications in quantum metrology and computing. Ultimately, this study contributes to our understanding of the interplay between intrinsic correlations and topological properties in quantum systems, which is an essential area of research in contemporary quantum physics. By analyzing on-shell and off-shell production, we can make in-depth predictions about the Higgs boson's width and non-standard interactions, including heavy vector boson exchange loops. Additionally, we explore the Higgs boson's unusual couplings with heavy quarks, charged leptons, and gluons, which could be significant at low four-lepton invariant masses due to heavy particle contributions. The proposed technique employs a hierarchical, multi-layered neural network to analyze spectral and spatial characteristics of image pixels as distinct features. By combining these features into a single representation, the autoencoder effectively captures complex alterations within the image. Through optimization, the latent space enables unsupervised clustering of altered pixels. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through comprehensive experiments conducted on synthetic and real-world hyperspectral imagery, which reveals its superiority to alternative unsupervised alteration detection methods. Furthermore, we showcase the potential of our method to identify alterations in diverse HSBI applications. The proposed technique contributes to the expansion of alteration detection methods to deal with data-scarce situations often encountered in practical hyperspectral imagery analysis. Quantum physics combines with advanced materials science to create exotic quantum phenomena, as seen in silicon's atomic-scale dimers, which feature a unique quantum spin gap. Utilizing a scanning tunneling microscopy technique, researchers have observed the transfer of angular momentum between two silicon atoms in a quantum valley state. Additionally, they have created a highly entangled state of spin and valley properties within a single dimer by exposing a silicon atom to a ruby laser pulse, triggering the transition from a spin-triplet to a spin-singlet state. The degree of entanglement is quantified using a measure called entanglement bias, which is highly dependent on the quantum valley state's properties. These observations indicate that valley interaction is the primary mechanism driving the transfer of spin, as the involvement of one valley state alone is insufficient to explain the data. These findings mark the first observation of spin transfer between two silicon atoms in a quantum valley state, opening up new avenues for the study of quantum entanglement in highly stable silicon dimer pairs. Furthermore, these results raise the possibility of manipulating a single electron's spin, using the transfer of angular momentum between two quantum valley states, which could serve as an innovative approach to achieving spin-polarization in silicon-based quantum devices. The valley interaction in these results provides valuable insight into designing novel quantum devices, particularly those using silicon macromolecules where valley degree of freedom acts as an inherent protection mechanism against decoherence. Lastly, these observations demonstrate the capability of tuning quantum pairs within a solid state by utilizing intense laser pulses, which could be a pivotal future tool in designing and testing quantum principles. The transfer of spin, observed here, serves as an innovative example of this capability, which may be used in future research to replicate extra-terrestrial experiments, such as testing Bell's inequality across large distances. Ultimately, these findings mark a significant milestone in our understanding of quantum physics in solids, which may soon enable the development of quantum-based communication networks. The data presented here is likely to be applicable to a broader range of materials, as the involved physics principles are highly transferable. However, soft optimization techniques often present significant complexity in terms of design, implementation, and experimentation, mainly due to the diverse range of problems they address and varying requirements such as feature vector extraction, embedding space construction, and nearest neighbor search.  There is currently no comprehensive, flexible framework available to facilitate the development and evaluation of novel software solutions to these problems, leading to a lack of open-source tools and repositories for benchmarking purposes. LibOPT comprises a set of open-source tools providing flexible, modular software solutions to optimization challenges, and related design, implementation, and performance analysis for future research and development in the field of optimization. We have developed a novel technique known as two-photon absorption boundary transient-current method, and we utilize it to study charge transport within single-crystalline diamond. By employing a femtosecond laser oscillator with adjustable pulse duration and power, we create a two-photon process in the diamond, and as charge carriers are generated, we monitor the movement of these carriers across the crystal's length, conducting our experiments under air conditions. Our results indicate notably long charge carrier recombination times - over a hundred nanoseconds, and we have broken down these times into components using a complex model. These findings are unprecedented for diamond charge transport research. If our results are confirmed, they will suggest that diamond could be an attractive material for high-power high-frequency electronics due to its exceptionally conductive properties. Additionally, we discuss how the structure of our device allows for the study of charge transport within a specific region of the diamond, and the potential this holds for exploring unique properties in semiconductor materials. Lastly, we acknowledge the limitations of our model, particularly its lack of consideration for carrier escape, and we plan to improve our research by incorporating this factor in future models. Nonetheless, our work today offers an innovative approach to understanding charge transport within materials, and it enables the investigation of unique phenomena in semiconductors that were previously inaccessible to study. Finally, we emphasize that the principles behind our technique can be adapted for use in other materials, and we look forward to continuing this line of research to explore various other materials. Additionally, we successfully demonstrate the transient currents generated by the diamond in real-time using our custom-built amplifier system. Although we chose a relatively weak laser source for our experiments, we have recorded current levels as high as 100 milliamperes, and we have measured the transient currents' rise to approximately ten percent of that peak. Nonetheless, a significant portion of our data remains unrecorded due to current limitations of our detection equipment and detector amplification difficulties. Thus, we have developed and successfully tested a novel technique known as two-photon absorption boundary transient-current method for studying charge transport within single-crystalline diamond. This technique allows us to monitor charge carriers as they move across the crystal's length and offers an innovative approach to understanding charge transport within materials, and it enables the investigation of unique properties in semiconductors that were previously inaccessible to study. This framework, known as PMC-Learn, is based on the probabilistic model checkers PRISM and PSL, allowing it to leverage advanced model checking techniques during controller training. By integrating learning controllers in model-driven systems, we can improve their robustness against unforeseen events and scenarios. A primary goal of this research is to ensure the controllers developed can operate safely and efficiently without relying on precise system models. These results validate the potential of PMC-Learn as a tool for developing adaptable controllers that can respond robustly to a range of situations. This research paves the way for further exploration into the development of learning controllers that can adapt to changing system environments. We have shown that the Scott framework's partiality can be accommodated within univalent type theory by employing a non-injective version of the latter. To achieve this, we first developed a non-injective version of the Scott information system as a poset within the framework of set theory in type theory. Following this, we extended the Scott framework's denotational semantics for PCF to type theory, preserving the original's full abstraction properties. Notably, the primary challenge in this adaptation was addressing the issues posed by equality in type theory, specifically through the management of "twist" factors as well as the poset's non-strictness. Ultimately, we were able to formulate an abstract theorem that captures the full abstractness of the Scott framework's semantics for PCF within type theory, by expressing the relationship between any two poset homomorphisms whose composition forms an embedding. As a key result, the poset's non-strictness proved to be unnecessary, thus allowing us to apply the same reasoning that shows the full abstractness of the original PCF denotational semantics directly to the present case. Finally, we have verified that the key results of this study can also be applied to full abstractions in type theory with a fundamental ordering. Contrary to earlier beliefs that posets in type theory are too restrictive to facilitate a meaningful discussion of denotational semantics, we believe that the current findings provide a strong foundation for further exploration into the domain of information systems within type theory.

A longstanding problem in combinatorial optimization, posed by Turan in 1941, has to do with finding the minimum number of edges in a triangle-free graph with a specific chromatic number. Exoo and Levitt recently made significant progress on this issue by narrowing down the possible solutions, and in this research we provide a new lower bound for the minimum number of edges in a triangle-free graph. Our result resolves Turan's challenge by showing that any such graph must have at least $\frac{n}{6} + o(n)$ edges, where $n$ represents the graph's number of vertices. This answer confirms a conjecture made by Bollobas in the 1960s. Furthermore, our proof by projection reveals a relationship between this problem and another optimization issue, and from that, a related packing challenge. By examining the latter problem, we derive our lower bound. An interesting consequence of our work is the confirmation of a hypothesis made by Alon, Friedgut, and Tszeng in the late 1990s, stating that for any given positive $\epsilon$, there exists a natural number $c$ such that in any $n$-vertex triangle-free graph with C edges, the $\epsilon$-deviation graph will contain an isolated vertex. Additionally, for any given double $0 < \epsilon < 1$, we obtain a precise value for c, and this answer resolves the Turan tetrahedron challenge for the $\ell_2$-norm. Also, our research yields an optimal solution to a problem in extremal combinatorics by deriving the extremal property of triangle-free graphs with the minimum number of edges. In map display, especially when zoomed in on vector maps, line junctions can lead to a rasterization effect known as aliasing, which diminishes the quality of visual representations. Traditional anti-aliasing techniques have primarily been designed for raster displays and are either ineffective or computationally demanding when applied to map rendering. This study introduces an enhanced spatial anti-aliasing method specifically for line junctions, achieved through a straightforward calculation using the map's coordinate system. This novel technique not only surpasses existing solutions but also accommodates various alpha blending modes to facilitate a range of visual rendering techniques. Furthermore, our research demonstrates that this algorithm can be efficiently implemented while maintaining high performance. The effectiveness of this algorithm is exemplified through a series of practical rendering examples, which showcase its ability to produce high-quality map visualization with minimal computation. Our anti-aliasing method has been successfully applied in several prominent map applications since 2015. A new family of transcendental radial basis functions is presented along with a corresponding quasi-interpolation formula, which retains its linear independence. The proposed function maintains optimal approximation properties in a straightforward manner. Specifically, the operator preserves linear and quadratic polynomials, in addition to being weakly singular with respect to one derivative. The underlying idea is then adapted to higher-order piecewise polynomial spaces, from a single variable to multiple variable scenario. The primary aim of this study is to address the primary limitation of earlier RBF quasi-interpolation schemes, which often suffer from ill-conditioning. The proposed method is demonstrated to have a well-conditioned interpolation matrix in both theoretical and practical contexts. The study further validates the efficacy of the resulting operator using a series of numerical experiments spanning diverse datasets. The performance of these operators is ultimately compared to the established Wright-Gauss-Seidel method. The underlying theoretical findings are then substantiated by a set of numerical test cases. The results show that the new RBF quasi-interpolation scheme significantly outperforms the Wright-Gauss-Seidel method in terms of conditioning. The corresponding numerical error estimates for each interpolation method are presented, along with a detailed analysis of their convergence rates. The ultimate goal is to develop a highly conditioned and versatile RBF quasi-interpolation scheme that can effectively approximate multivariate functions with varying smoothness characteristics. The proposed method is expected to have far-reaching implications in multiple fields, including approximation theory, function spaces, and partial differential equations. To address this, researchers have been introducing various modifications to optimization algorithms, however the underlying problem of generalization remains poorly understood. In this study, we revisit the fundamental question of how to define an optimization algorithm that can be universally applied to any nonconvex loss function. To this end, we propose the Organic Gradient Descent (OGD) method, an intuitive and straightforward approach that is inspired by evolutionary principles. Notably, we prove that any OGD algorithm based on a specific class of convex functions can be adapted to optimize any nonconvex loss function, and our results also apply to subgradient methods, thus covering a broad range of existing optimization algorithms. Furthermore, we demonstrate an OGDC variant that is parameter-free and converges to a local minimum. Our comprehensive experiments show that OGDC can yield superior performance compared to established baselines in various machine learning tasks. The source J2102+6015 is a very powerful and distant object classified as a blazar, however, not all high-energy emissions can be attributed to blazar activity as they also originate from other non-thermal objects such as weak radio-loud quasars. By conducting detailed spectral analysis across multiple wavelengths, researchers have gathered evidence refuting the blazar hypothesis in favor of a quasar explanation. Their findings indicate the quasar's high-energy emissions are consistent with the emission spectrum of an object undergoing rapid growth, supporting a less complex interpretation. Moreover, their analysis reveals two components contributing to the quasar's emissions: a centrally located region producing most of the high-energy emissions and a larger area surrounding the core, contributing to lower frequency emissions.
