We undertook a comprehensive study of disk galaxies within groups and clusters that exhibited unique, 'U' shaped galactic warps. Our research expanded upon previous investigations by extensively sampling these galaxies, collecting data through spectroscopy on 82 objects, including newly discovered patterns in their distribution. Our findings reveal that group/cluster galaxies tend to be more tightly clustered and have larger galactic warps than those found in isolated environments. This leads us to suggest three possible theories: (i) high velocity gas collisions within groups, causing disk distortion; (ii) group members sharing similar orbits, resulting in similar warp shapes; and (iii) a gravitational interaction between galaxies, causing disk deformation. Additionally, our analysis links the massive, transformed galaxy, IC1101W, with other distorted galaxies, like Mrk 1483 and IC3727, categorizing them as 'jellyfish galaxies'. Our work paves the way for further exploration into the characteristics of jellyfish galaxies through spectroscopic observation. Jellyfish galaxies, such as IC1101W, are transformed through Fornax cluster interactions, with major distortions and Hα emission distributions. They can be classified into three types: those with blue optical colors and dominant Hα emission; those with red optical colors and no Hα emission; or those with peculiar red+blue colors and ongoing star formation. Studying these galaxies may reveal the processes behind their unique, spiral arms and contribute to understanding galaxy evolution, particularly the relationship between galaxy interactions, star formation, and spiral arm formation. Ultimately, our research may facilitate early jellyfish galaxy detection, allowing for timely observation of their formation from group to cluster phase. In the near future, this may lead to the identification of galaxies similar to IC1101W, but earlier in their evolution. Using existing data on 245 galactic candidates, we have developed a distinct selection method, based on their unique, 'U' shaped warp shape, to predict the presence of jellyfish galaxies in upcoming spectroscopic surveys, such as the SDSS-V, with potentially over 100 galactic candidates. In a companion paper, we will explore jellyfish galaxies with unambiguous blue Hα emission and investigate their formation through Fornax cluster interactions. This research may reveal the role of gas interactions, star formation, and spiral arm formation in these galaxies. As a result, our study may facilitate early detection of jellyfish galaxies, potentially shedding light on their formation from group to cluster phase. To this end, we are conducting a time-critical observation of jellyfish galaxies

Compounds composed of potassium ($A=$ K, Rb, Cs) combined with boron in a 2:1 ratio, exhibit unique characteristics linked to their vibrational modes. Notably, these vibrational modes display an anomalous heat capacity at low temperatures, which can be attributed to a specific phonon mode. Our study aimed to identify the origin of this phenomenon and discovered that it is influenced by a chiral vibrational mode present in the cubic structure of the compounds. This mode is characterized by an optically inactive transverse frequency and exists due to the time-reversal symmetry being compensated by a specific atomic arrangement. Using a symmetry analysis, we were able to determine the chiral vibrational mode's frequency and displacement patterns in relation to the atomic elements. These findings indicate that the chiral vibrational mode acts as a soft mode at zero Kelvin, and its condensation at a critical temperature can explain the observed heat capacity anomaly. Additionally, we calculated the dynamical properties of the chiral vibrational mode, and through density functional perturbation theory, we simulated x-ray scattering spectra, which revealed that the chiral vibrational mode's density of states corresponds to the experimental heat capacity data. This successful correlation solidifies the idea that the chiral vibrational mode's softening is responsible for the anomalous heat capacity at low temperatures. Finally, we explored other possible phonon modes that could potentially contribute to the heat capacity; however, it is evident that the chiral vibrational mode is the primary mode governing the heat capacity behavior. These findings provide a comprehensive understanding of the dynamic properties of this unique family of materials. Based on our analysis, we propose that the cubic structure's chiral nature is a universal feature, which we verified through electron density analysis. It is also interesting to note that the chiral nature is preserved when the materials transform into a tetragonal phase under applied pressure. Consequently, the concept of chirality can be applied not only to dynamics but also to static electron properties, which has significant implications in this research area. Overall, our study demonstrates that the dynamic chiral degree of freedom is an inherent property of the cubic materials in question, which may also be present in other materials exhibiting similar $A$B$_{2}$ structures. In 1941, Kolmogorov proposed a theory for unsuppressed fluid flow, stating that the energy spectrum and velocity gradient at a great distance from the source of the disturbance are largely unaffected by its origin. However, this theory failed to account for energy production and dissipation within the context. We present a new model, incorporating these elements in a highly irregular, turbulent-dissipative environment. The model separates the energy hierarchy into distinct layers, triggering an interaction-free, inert interface at a specific scale. Unlike Kolmogorov's hypothesis, our new simulation excludes the assumption of smooth, wave-like fluctuations, yielding a unique understanding of the energy structure throughout the turbulence range. Consequently, the simulated fluid behavior exhibits an extremely complex and self-similar pattern. By applying our new simulation, we clarify the long-standing debate regarding the energy consumption in the turbulence range and the nature of the fluid fluctuations. Furthermore, our study provides an innovative explanation for the apparent stability of the liquid surface in the middle of a breaking droplet's collapse, triggered by an unusually viscous and turbulent state in that specific scenario. Lastly, the study presents an analytical expression governing the height of the fluid fluctuations in both the far-reaching and close-up perspectives. Specifically, at a great distance from the fluid source, the scale of the fluctuations is determined by the balance between energy consumption and the rate of energy consumption, whereas at a close-up perspective, the scale of the fluctuations is entirely controlled by the energy consumption. By contrast, the energy structure in the very close-up perspective is shaped by an equilibrium between energy production and the rate of energy consumption. Consequently, our new simulation predicts a relationship between the liquid surface fluctuation size and a particular combination of the fluid's viscosity and the rate of energy consumption, thereby capturing an essential, previously unaccounted-for feature of the fluid dynamics. This phenomenon is seen in materials exhibiting Witten effect, which are characterized by half-integer spin. To identify the sources of the topological magnetoelectric effect, a detailed analysis was conducted across a spectrum of 3D topological systems, including chiral fermion, weak topological, strong topological, and topological free fermion models. In each case, the topological magnetoelectric effect was found to originate from edge or surface states with half-integer spin. Edge states of these systems were then linked to a nonlinear time-reversal-invariant response, which provides an alternative means of detection. The connection between the topological magnetoelectric effect and the half-integer quantum Hall effect was also established, along with examples demonstrating the realization of these phenomena in various models. Additionally, key findings were translated into Witten effect and topological magnetoelectric effect invariant signatures via boundary responses under time-reversal and spatial inversion. Lastly, a key observation was made regarding the relationship between the half-integer quantum Hall effect and the geometric magnetoelectric effect: the latter can exist without the former, as illustrated through a topological free fermion model example. Overall, this research contributes to understanding the geometric magnetoelectric effect, opening doors for new experimental and theoretical explorations. We investigate the semantics of the random lambda-calculus, an extension of the lambda-calculus designed to handle non-deterministic computations and infinite data, often found in computations with the oracle Turing machine. Insufficient previous studies had focused on the semantics of this calculus due to methodological restrictions, such as requiring only finitely many parallel computations. However, these studies didn't take into account all relevant aspects of the calculus. In contrast, we develop two different semantics for the full random lambda-calculus and show that these semantics have been understudied. One semantics, of limited use, relies on measures, while another, more applicable, relies on probabilities. In conclusion, we provide a new perspective on the theoretical underpinnings of the random lambda-calculus, by inspecting its relationship with existing theories. Design communication often relies on diverse formats such as texts, images, and 3D models, which designers discuss and merge through dialogue to facilitate collaborative design. Although design communication has long been verbal, recent advancements in natural language processing technology have made text the dominant format in recent years. However, design communication would be more efficient if all participants could view and interact with each other's content equally. Therefore, a unified platform for design communication is required that supports various formats and allows designers to communicate effectively through text. This paper presents a study of design communication through text within the engineering design field, analyzing the conclusions drawn by designers based on their counterparts' content representations to identify relationships between design communication and product development strategies. Design communication was found to be consistent for teams working on a particular project but varied significantly between different design projects. Moreover, designers tend to draw bold conclusions when designing products from scratch rather than evolving or refining existing designs. Additionally, designers tend to conclude design communications more frequently with 2D representations than with other formats. Finally, this study shows that designers tend to conclude design communications more frequently when designing products partially from scratch rather than when refining or improving existing designs. A mining approach that evaluates design communication as a whole and not project-by-project has been proposed to support designers in making more informed decisions during design communication. In other words, designers would be advised to be more cautious with design communication as a whole but designers would also be advised to be more bold when designing products partially from scratch. Furthermore, designers would be advised to be more cautious when designing products from 2D representations only. Finally, with design communication as a whole, designers would be advised to be more cautious when designing products when compared with existing products. An experiment was also conducted to validate the proposed approach, which showed promising results. An approach was developed to measure robust conclusion of design communication by evaluating the consistency of design communication as a whole. As a result, an alternative approach was proposed that evaluates design communication by considering various content representations and their corresponding strategies. Moreover, designers were found to draw bold conclusions when designing products from scratch, designing products partially from scratch, and designing products from 2D representations only. For a proximal gradient method applied to a nonconvex optimization problem, its iterative sequence converges to a stationary point. To generalize this, we consider an optimization problem with a possibly nonconvex objective function and a parameterized manifold of solutions. We investigate a specific reparameterization of this manifold using a proximal point method, analyzing its convergence. This convergence result is akin to those obtained in the convex case, revealing that the reparameterization converges to a stationary point within the manifold when using an unbiased sampling approach, and further converges to a stationary point when combined with a specific averaging procedure. We illustrate the effectiveness of these general convergence results via geometric optimization problems, such as finding extremal points on manifolds, and further show that these results can be applied to analyzing the convergence of implicit smoothing methods for nonsmooth optimization problems. Specifically, we examine a nonconvex optimization problem involving a composition of convex functions. When applying a proximal point method to this problem, its iterative sequence converges to a stationary point within the implicit smoothing manifold of solutions. We also consider an explicit smoothing approach for a special case of nonconvex optimization problems involving a matrix variable, and analyze its convergence to a stationary point within the implicit smoothing manifold of solutions. Our analysis reveals that these general convergence results can be also applied to analyzing the convergence of implicit smoothing methods for nonsmooth optimization problems. The numerical experiments presented in this study demonstrate that the implicit smoothing method can be more robust and efficient than proximal gradient flow in some nonconvex optimization problems. In particular, we test this method on an optimization problem involving a matrix variable whose objective function is a nonconvex sum of convex functions. When applying the implicit smoothing method to this problem, its iterative sequence converges to a stationary point within the implicit smoothing manifold of solutions. The specific averaging procedure used in this problem yields a stationary point that is closer to the global optimum than the stationary points obtained by proximal gradient flow and another smoothing method, which are two commonly employed methods in this context. As a result, the implicit smoothing method is able to achieve better convergence results than these two other methods. Furthermore, our analysis shows that the implicit smoothing method is able to recover the known stationary points of a convex optimization problem involving a matrix variable when its smoothing parameter tends to a specific value. In particular, we consider an optimization problem involving a log-det heuristic for matrix manifold, and apply an implicit smoothing method to this problem, yielding a stationary point within the log-det heuristic manifold of solutions. This work outlines our plan to leverage the unique characteristics of photonic devices to address two key challenges in cross-matching spectral observations. Firstly, we will develop innovative solutions to streamline the cross-matching process for large datasets. Secondly, we will design new photonic devices capable of accurately matching spectral observations, even those with limited data quality or noisy spectra. By drawing inspiration from the field of medicine, we refer to these approaches as 'astrophotonic remedies.' As a starting point, we will draw upon previous research involving dispersion devices, before introducing novel designs for phased arrays based on generalized eponymous thin films. These devices have the potential to facilitate single-stage cross-matching of spectral observations and enable the development of user-friendly, compact astrophotonic devices for cross-matching applications. Additionally, we will explore the feasibility of integrating photonics, electronics, and software within a single device to facilitate interactive cross-matching, thereby bridging the gap between laboratory photonics and astrophotonic devices capable of delivering meaningful results to astronomers. By addressing these challenges through photonic innovation, we believe that 'astrophotonic remedies' have the power to transform the field of spectral cross-matching and ultimately contribute to more efficient astronomical research and discovery. The increasing reliance on multiple medications compels the healthcare system to ensure their combined safety, posing a challenge for existing methods to assess medication interactions. In this paper, we offer an integrated outlook on relational deep learning in medication pairing, highlighting its benefits and addressing common criticisms. To tackle the complex issue of drug interactions, a novel relational graph attention network is proposed, taking into consideration the distinct requirements of each interaction direction (unidirectional vs. bidirectional). Experimental evaluations on widely used benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of existing relational deep learning approaches, with notable improvements seen in specific datasets. However, our proposed network did not outperform other methods in comprehensive tests. Nonetheless, this survey's findings serve as a foundation for future research on bidirectional medication interactions, and its code is accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/wzhe6396/MedScorer.

Several countries are now adopting the use of computer vision for road damage detection and identification, but the advancement of this technology in various nations is hindered due to a lack of local dataset availability. For more developed countries like Germany, there are numerous high-quality datasets available that support the training of sophisticated deep learning models. In contrast, countries like India lack such datasets, leading to slower progress in this field. To bridge this disparity, this study proposes a pioneering approach that enables the adaptation of advanced road damage identification models to new environments using transfer learning. The development of a groundbreaking, open-source damage classification annotation tool driven by deep learning simplifies the annotation process of Indian roads, resulting in the creation of the first comprehensive and high-quality dataset for urban Indian roads. Furthermore, a detailed evaluation of the effectiveness of deep learning models on various Indian cities was conducted, revealing that models pre-trained on German data can be fine-tuned on in-service Indian data to achieve exceptional performance. The proposed technique has the potential to accelerate the deployment of this technology in numerous developing countries where a lack of local data exists. Imitation learning seeks to bypass extensive game-based data collection by instead training agents to replicate human actions, but its success depends on having multiple trajectories across various areas of the state space. This can be a limitation for complex, partially observable tasks where such diversity is hard to achieve. In this research, we present a new method to overcome this limitation by using raw visual data of a demonstration space and generating diverse trajectories across different sub-spaces using unsupervised learning techniques. We test the proposed approach on a set of 2D and 3D navigation tasks with partially observable environments and compare its effectiveness against existing methods. The experimental results show that our method outperforms existing approaches in efficiently replicating goal-oriented behaviors from a limited number of demonstrations. Association rules are widely used in Data Mining for analyzing data sets to draw customer-oriented conclusions. The technical concepts underlying association rules are related to Boolean functions, hypergraphs, and binary data. This research focuses on finding the smallest possible base, which is essentially the smallest set of association rules capable of reproducing the original data through a process similar to resolution. This paper introduces new frameworks for generating association rules, incorporating elements of negation and abstraction to improve efficiency. Unlike previous methods, our approach does not require the calculation of frequent itemsets, which can be computationally expensive. By leveraging deduction frameworks, we are able to derive association rules directly from data, without first finding all frequent itemsets. This enables minimum-size-base generation to be accomplished in linear time, except for one special case, which takes quadratic time. To validate our approach, we performed experiments using real-world data, which show that our method outperforms existing techniques. This research provides strong evidence that our proposed frameworks are suitable for practical applications and offers promising avenues for further exploration. Additionally, our results indicate that the concepts of confidence, support, and anti-support can be effectively utilized in association rule analysis. To demonstrate the versatility of our approach, we are able to extend the concepts of hypergraphs and deduction frameworks to cover more general cases, such as weighted data, hypergraphs with weights, and hypergraphs that incorporate negation. This research showcases the wide range of related problems to established mathematical concepts, including the Cayley-Kitzelback theorem, Lagrange's four-square theorem, the Pythagorean theorem, the fundamental theorem of arithmetic, and Combinatorics. Ultimately, this research provides a thorough mathematical analysis of association rule generation, which can serve as a valuable reference for future studies in this field. Mental afflictions significantly contribute to the high representation of individuals with mental disorders within the criminal justice system. This is compounded by limited access to mental healthcare, leading to troubling consequences for those struggling. A unique opportunity to improve mental healthcare and its connection to the justice system arises from court-ordered therapy for convicted individuals. To explore the potential of this opportunity, we conducted a study analyzing data covering nearly 20 years involving the convictions and health conditions of over 1 million individuals in Florida. Our research revealed that although court-ordered therapy is associated with improved mental health, its benefits are limited to those who complete the program. Furthermore, this analysis uncovered specific conditions and risk factors that predict a higher likelihood of program completion. Notably, our findings show that individuals with a lower income are less likely to complete the program. These results suggest that enhancing mental healthcare within the justice system could have a positive impact on both the justice system and the healthcare sector. Ultimately, increasing the program's completion rate holds the key to improving the mental well-being of this demographic. Given that millions of people pass through the justice system each year, scaling the program's success on a larger scale could result in substantial cost savings for the healthcare and justice systems, promoting a more efficient allocation of funds between these sectors. Additionally, this could lead to widespread adoption, empowering more judges to require therapy as a means of making informed, justice-reform decisions that prioritize individual mental health. In essence, our research offers a data-driven model capable of addressing two pressing issues: the growing mental healthcare needs and the financial strain on the justice system. Thus, this study aims to contribute to the ongoing conversation regarding the relationship between mental healthcare and the justice system by providing a practical, quantifiable solution to improve the lives of individuals within this demographic and ultimately the broader justice community. Given the scope and scale of our findings, our recommendations have the potential to be replicated in various locations, facilitating widespread adoption and dissemination. Therefore, we invite mental health professionals, justice system officials, and community leaders to utilize our research as a practical guide for enhancing the mental healthcare of convicted individuals. This method is particularly relevant to processes governed by strict timelines, such as medical conditions following a specific timeline of progression, and it is also relevant to anomaly detection more broadly. The emergence of differential privacy has provided a framework for constructing confidential statistical estimators, although traditional methods may not be sufficient when dealing with dependent data such as time-series data. One-sided differential privacy offers a potential solution, providing a more statistics-friendly and data-efficient approach than the conventional method. However, the confidentiality breach issue in dependent data under this framework has not been thoroughly explored. This research investigates the confidentiality breach issue in dependent data, specifically focusing on the case of recursive structural equations. Several dependent data scenarios are examined, including the effects of block-length, recursion depth, and conventional differential privacy. The findings demonstrate that the confidentiality breach rate under the one-sided differential privacy schedule is significantly higher than that under the conventional differential privacy schedule, particularly in certain dependent data scenarios. While the overall rate of breach is low, the confidentiality breach rate can be substantial when data are extremely sensitive. This rate can be influenced by various parameters such as recursion depth and block-length. To further contextualize these findings, several examples of sensitive data have been used. Finally, the effectiveness of the hypothesis testing methodology for dependent data under the conventional differential privacy schedule has been evaluated. The results show that the standard methodology becomes suboptimal when data are dependent and that a different testing approach is required. This research also explores alternative confidentiality breach schedules, revealing that the inverse polynomial schedule yields the most favorable outcome in terms of confidentiality breach rate. The proposed methodology is an innovative contribution that has not been previously explored in research. Additionally, several promising directions for future research have been identified. Gallium nitride (GaN) is a promising material for high-power electronics due to its potential to operate at extremely low temperatures and high temperatures, however, its application in power devices is hindered by low hole mobility at room temperature. Past research has found that substituting germanium (Ge) and magnesium (Mg) into the GaN lattice enhances the mobility by reducing lattice strain through the relaxation of tetragonal distortion. To investigate this further, theoretical models and first-principles calculations are employed to explore the structural, electrical and elastic properties of Ga$_{1-x-y}$Mg$_x$Ge$_y$N$_2$ and find that introducing a pair of substitutional defects results in a significant improvement of hole mobility along the c-axis of hexagonal GaN, increasing by 150% when aligned with ZnGeN$_2$ and by 110% when aligned with MgSiN$_2$, exceeding current experimental values. Furthermore, it is discovered that the general rule governing the strain healing effect in these materials can be described by the elastic anisotropy, $A\sigma_{xx}\epsilon_{yy}$, where a high anisotropy factor is necessary for strain healing in these materials, and that introducing a second acceptor defect (SiN$_2$) has a marginal effect but always supports the strain healing effect in GaN. These theoretical findings indicate that strain engineering using the II-IV-N$_2$ family of compounds is a viable method for further research to further boost hole mobility in GaN. Ultimately, low temperature (LHe) and high temperature (HT) experiments are suggested to verify the theoretical predictions made here. Additionally, incorporating the accepted values of dielectric constant from GaN would result in hole mobility enhancements of 120% (vs. ZnGeN$_2$) and 90% (vs. MgSiN$_2$), under the assumption that the tetragonal distortion is the sole contributor to the lattice strain in these materials. In recent years, link prediction in temporal knowledge graphs (TKGs) has gained significant interest. Most existing approaches focus on incorporating temporal information by embedding two separate vectors for each knowledge entity, one for each time point. However, this can lead to the issue of model interpretability and increased model complexity. To address this challenge, we propose an innovative method that leverages static vector frameworks for TKG link forecasting. By embedding a single static vector for each knowledge entity, our approach simplifies the model architecture while maintaining comparable performance to more complex models. Experimental results on three real-world datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms the baseline static model, with a substantial improvement of at least 11% on four challenging configurations when combined with hard attention techniques. Notably, our approach performs competitively on a soft attention setup, with a gap of no more than 5% compared to harder attention methods. Additionally, our approach performs well under temporal distribution shift scenarios, with a maximum performance drop of 20%. The code and generated embeddings are available on GitHub for reproducibility purposes.

Fragmentation of a heavy quark into a heavy quark bound state, specifically the D-meson, in a medium with non-zero temperature and magnetic field is being investigated using a propagator framework. This framework is capable of imaging the internal structure of heavy quarks across various momentum configurations. At a finite magnetic field, the fragmentation process exhibits symmetry breaking in momentum distribution, which contradicts the situation without a magnetic field. Notably, in the rest frame of the fragmentation plane, an anisotropic distribution is observed in momentum space, particularly in the direction transverse to the jet flow. This anisotropy is found to be influenced by the mass of bound quarks and temperature of the medium. As a result, different internal structures of heavy quark bound states can be distinguished through analysis of transverse anisotropy. Additionally, by comparing properties of long-range, oscillating components and short-range components, it is being induced that interactions between quarks and the medium with magnetic field can alter the internal structures of heavy quark bound states. This research is an extension of prior studies at zero temperature and magnetic field. They are expecting to see similar effects in experiments like the RHIC and LHC. We present a novel approach that combines knowledge graph embeddings with language models to address question answering challenges. Our method involves training a language model to predict a knowledge graph path based on a given question, using a language-specific decoder to convert the question into a knowledge graph query. To improve this process, we propose multiple innovations, including the use of multiple candidate paths in prediction, and the integration of answer and entity selection tasks. Experimental evaluations demonstrate the efficacy of our method, with notable success in ZMQP and Natural Questions datasets. Specifically, our method achieves 44.4% F1 score on the ZMQP dataset, outperforming the top-performing transformer model by 11.1%. Additionally, our method 2nd-place finishes in the Natural Questions dataset in the GQA challenge 2020. Code and pre-trained models can be found on our GitHub repository. 

Knowledge graph prediction models have shown exceptional ability to process questions with varying lengths and interpret semantic meanings. Moreover, the ability of these models to generate multiple candidate paths in response to questions provides valuable information for evaluating their accuracy. Despite these capabilities, it remains challenging to directly apply these models in question answering tasks that rely on text fields, due to issues related to the interpretation of question tokens as knowledge graph entities. 

To address this limitation, we propose a simple yet effective solution, involving the conversion of questions into a knowledge graph query, using a language-specific decoder, and the prediction of a knowledge graph path based on this query. When evaluating multiple candidate paths, the model demonstrates exceptional question answering capabilities. Building on this idea, we have integrated the answer and entity selection tasks into a single joint training process. Experimental results confirm the effectiveness of this approach, with notable success in question answering challenges. 

We first evaluated our proposed model, Fine-Tune-KGE, on the ZMQP dataset. The results indicate that a model that uses the Complex ER model, processed through a language model, and predicts a single path, performs better than top-ranking transformer models. Specifically, our model achieves 44.4% F1 score, surpassing the top-performing transformer model by 11.1%. When evaluating multiple candidate paths, the model performs even better, with an F1 score of 46.3%. 

In addition to evaluating our model on the ZMQP dataset, we also analyzed its capabilities on the Natural Questions dataset in the GQA challenge 2020. The results show that our model places 2nd among participating teams.

We have developed a novel high-dimensional expander graph construction, utilizing coverings of certain finite simplicial complexes with geometric properties. This graph, the Cayley complex $\Gamma$, possesses a rigid structure that ensures its vanishing of top-dimensional faces and specific isolation of lower-dimensional faces, resulting from projections of high-dimensional vectors. From this, we derive expander graphs by selecting particular vertex subsets from $\Gamma$ and demonstrating that these graphs exhibit the expander isomorphism theorem, a characteristic of high-dimensional expander graphs. This research yields numerous high-dimensional expander graphs in various settings, offering potential applications in group theory, geometry, and computer science. Specifically, we construct families of high-dimensional expander graphs based on the Cayley complex of certain finite groups, such as $SL_3(\F_q)$, and certain finite simplicial complexes with geometric properties, such as the flag complex of exponential size of certain finite fields. This research also offers partial answers to certain open problems in group theory and combinatorics. Furthermore, we devise a simple and efficient algorithm for generating high-dimensional expander graphs, offering a trade-off between the size of the graph and its connectivity. This research can be viewed under three different perspectives: the geometric structure of groups with a Zariski topology, the coverage of certain finite simplicial complexes, and the analysis of the random graph isomorphism problem. Finally, we investigate the interleukable graphs, which are derived from the Cayley complex $\Gamma$, and demonstrate that these graphs are, in fact, high-dimensional expanders. This research offers a simple and efficient algorithm for generating interleukable graphs, offering a trade-off between the size of the graph and its connectivity. This construction has applications in group theory, geometry, and computer science. This research can potentially be generalized to higher-dimensional settings, and we provide a outline of the possible generalization. Our analysis suggests that current language models struggle with non-trivial choices, but with data augmentation and more advanced models, their performance improves significantly. Early detection of liver cancer often relies on ultrasound screenings, which we've enhanced by combining deep learning with Rydberg atom technology. This novel approach uses Rydberg atoms to detect multifrequency microwave radiation, enabling unique patterns of excitation that distinguish between different tissue types. Unlike conventional Rydberg sensors, which require a confined environment, our Rydberg atom microscope can operate in an external setup, leveraging the atom's long-range dipole polarizability under near-resonant microwave drive. This enables highly sensitive detection of liver tissues' responses to specific microwave frequencies, which a deep learning algorithm subsequently analyzes to identify the target frequencies causing excitation. This multi-frequency microwave detection capability outperforms existing Rydberg sensors and conventional Rydberg atom microscopes by selectively activating multiple frequency channels, demonstrating superior wavelength selectivity, a broader detection range, and significantly lower noise levels. This progress brings Rydberg atom microscopes one step closer to surpassing conventional Rydberg sensors in performance. This research has led to a deep learning-trained Rydberg sensor that requires fewer atoms for comparable noise levels, and has set a noise floor for future deep learning-assisted Rydberg atom microscopes. This work is poised to expand the boundaries of Rydberg atom microscopes and deep learning technology alike. Analysis of gravity waves in Mars' atmosphere, particularly in the upper layer, is generally based on direct in situ observations which are scarce and limited to specific missions. To expand understanding, ground-based optical sensors on board spacecraft including MGS, ODY, MRO, and MAVEN were examined to assess gravity waves in Mars' thermospheric layer. These sensors measured gravity waves by calculating vertical or horizontal density vertical gradient, effectively extending the detection range to ~100 km in altitude. As a result, multiple gravity waves were detected in each mission's dataset, and the most prevalent waves were horizontally aligned with the planet's westward wind direction. The spatial distribution of these waves in the ODY and MRO datasets showed a seasonal pattern, with waves primarily occurring during the local winter months. The average interocular distance of these waves in the ODY and MRO datasets was approximately 3000 km, with the MAVEN dataset showing an average distance of around 1000 km. The amplitude of these gravity waves was observed to be in the range of 10 to 30 m/s, and the momentum flux of these waves was found to increase with altitude, ultimately contributing to escape from the planet's atmosphere. The presence of non-stationary gravity waves in each mission's dataset was confirmed through a combination of spectral and time-frequency analyses, and the movement of these waves was found to be influenced by the planet's wind patterns. In particular, the ground-based optical sensors on board MRO and MAVEN were observed to detect waves moving against the planet's wind direction at high altitudes, potentially contributing to atmospheric loss. To confirm this contribution, future studies should include in situ observations within the planet's magnetic tail, and assess the connection between gravity waves and atmospheric escape as observed through various spacecraft systems. In summary, this research examined the activity of gravity waves in each mission's dataset, and their impact on the planet's atmosphere, ultimately contributing to atmospheric loss. The analysis of gravity waves in each mission's dataset revealed distinct patterns and characteristics, and the detection of non-stationary gravity waves through a combination of spectral and time-frequency analyses confirmed prior observations. The findings of this research will contribute to future studies on board MARS, Parker, and Sample, as well as NASA's Mars Atmospheric Ions and Electrons (MAIE) and Mars Atmospheric Link to the Moon (MALM) missions. As a result, this research will help expand understanding of gravity waves in each mission's dataset, and their activity in each atmosphere, ultimately contributing to atmospheric loss.

The LHC holds the record for the highest energy particle collisions ever achieved, encompassing not only proton-proton impacts but also heavy ions over a broad range of energies, surpassing even the energy seen in cosmic ray phenomena. Specifically, the ALICE detector recorded lead-lead collisions at a staggering 5.02 TeV per nucleon pair, marking a significant breakthrough in ultra-peripheral collisions involving the exchange of highly virtual photons. These photon-photon interactions give rise to a range of exotic matter production, including charmonium-like states like the forward J/psi, which were extensively measured and analyzed across various rapidity ranges and transverse momentum thresholds. Concurrently, the production of these states offers a unique window into the study of photon-photon differential cross-sections, thereby aiding in the elucidation of underlying photonic structure. This research paper outlines the most recent findings on J/psi production in lead-lead collisions at 5.02 TeV in the 2.97-4.90 rapidity range with a transverse momentum above 3 GeV/c. The research further examines co-moving magnetic field influences on charmonium suppression at energy scales approaching the mass of these particles themselves (approximately 3.7 GeV). The analysis compares and integrates experimental data with the theoretical predictions of both non-relativistic and relativistic transport models. Moreover, the research explores the feasibility of using the ALICE detector to detect muon pairs resulting from the breakdown of the J/psi, which would significantly boost the detection rate by a factor of 10. To mitigate the severity of a pandemic, economists have advocated for timely and coordinated economic policies, arguing that delaying action leads to greater economic losses. Conversely, we contend that timely policies can minimize both health harms and economic damages. Notably, our analysis reveals that the optimal pandemic mitigation strategy is not a trade-off between health and economic goals, but rather a singular solution that simultaneously minimizes both health harms and economic losses. This comprehensive approach applies universally, independent of specific policy details or local conditions. We demonstrate that the finest policy timing is generally preferable, with deviations from the ideal frequency yielding suboptimal results, regardless of the specific policy type. Consequently, the best pandemic policies are those that prioritize timely execution over adaptation to evolving local conditions or policy preferences. Ultimately, our findings suggest that the most effective pandemic policies are those that are straightforward, universally applicable, and resistant to modification based on unfolding events or varying circumstances. Conversely, some pandemic policies may require adjustments in response to changing circumstances, such as lockdown durations that fluctuate in line with infection trends. We also maintain that critical interventions, including social distancing and vaccination, should be informed by scientific expertise rather than economic considerations. Finally, we observe that the widespread misuse of economic discrete-time models in pandemic research and policy discussions warrants more robust criticism and public awareness. These models can generate misleading, easily interpretable'statics' that can harm policy development, prompting a greater need to address their limitations and biases. Specifically, these models may fail to capture the significance of timing, the persistence of pandemic duration, and the irreversibility of both health harms and economic losses. We contend that the primary challenge is not reconciling conflicting values, but rather a lack of adequate information about the pandemic itself. We propose that a pressing unmet need is the development of a public 'pandemicon': a comprehensive, widely accessible guide that records our collective knowledge about the essential characteristics of effective pandemic policies. These characteristics, such as the importance of timely interventions, can be gleaned from our analytical results and the scientific literature. A pandemicon could serve as a unifying framework for ongoing research and existing knowledge, bridging the gap between experts and non-experts, and providing a shared understanding of the essential pandemic characteristics. We see this idea as an extension of the Statics project of the Center for Economic Studies and Methodology at the United Nations. The effectiveness of a machine learning model heavily relies on high-quality training data. However, data quality issues arise frequently and can go undetected until the training process begins, often requiring time-consuming data validation. We introduce an approach to proactively identify and mitigate data quality problems early on by integrating data troubleshooting into the machine learning development pipeline. During training, anomalies in the data are scored and their impact on model performance is measured, allowing for the rapid isolation and correction of problematic data. A set of user-configurable rules enables flexible anomaly detection and weighting strategies, facilitating the identification of significant data quality issues. We evaluate our method on real-world datasets from image classification, NLP, and recommendation systems, demonstrating its effectiveness in highlighting and addressing substantial data quality issues. Moreover, our code is openly accessible on GitHub for public use. By addressing data quality problems as they arise during machine learning development, resources that were previously devoted to model fine-tuning can be redirected towards data cleaning, ultimately leading to improved models and operating efficiency. A demonstration video of our method is available here: https://youtu.be/6Rr8R7hR9GQ. Experimental results and code can be found at: https://github.com/leonardosantini/data-troubleshooting. Additional results can be accessed at: https://aletheia-datachallenge.org/. This research is partially based on an earlier study that first introduced the concept of troubleshooting over end-to-end machine learning pipelines: Significance-driven Troubleshooting of Machine Learning Pipelines, Leonardi et al., 2022. This paper has received the Chair's Award at the 2022 IEEE International Conference on Advanced Learning Technologies. It has also been selected for a Virtual Oral Presentation at the 2022 NeurIPS Conference. In addition, two follow-up studies have been accepted for publication: Data Troubleshooting with Shapley Significance over End-to-End Machine Learning Pipelines, Santini et al., 2023; and Shapley: The Machine Learning Health Inspector, Bazzan et al., 2023. A recent study demonstrated that a small increase in pressure transforms Mn$_3$Sn's magnetic phases from a two-domain pattern to a single-domain pattern, causing a significant enhancement of the anomalous Hall effect. To address the issue of partisan gerrymandering in the United States, we developed an innovative approach combining intuitive geography and Monte Carlo methods, drawn from our previous research in simulated quenched systems. This technique leverages the principles of thermal free fermion systems to assess the fairness of electoral boundaries. We applied this method to the 2016 US presidential election results in Ohio, focusing on the state's congressional district elections. Our analysis took into account the typical sources of inaccuracy associated with this technique, such as irregular survey sampling, for the purpose of creating a more accurate statistical test. This testing revealed clear evidence of unfair electoral boundaries benefiting the Republican party. We found significant disparities in the probabilities of Democratic victories, 0.690 for the actual district elections, and 0.500 for randomly drawn ones, across the state's 16 congressional districts. Furthermore, our analysis showed that the likelihood of Democratic victories was consistently lower in districts drawn by the Republican legislature (0.690) compared to those drawn by federal courts (0.594) or by neutral algorithms (0.576). We found that the electoral boundaries in Ohio consistently fell short of a 95% confidence threshold for naturally obtained election results. This gross injustice highlights the effectiveness of our method in detecting unfair electoral boundaries and provides a promising framework for addressing gerrymandering in the United States. Given its reliance on election results and geographical boundaries, this technique can be applied to assess the fairness of electoral boundaries at the local, state, or national levels. Finally, this approach is compatible with existing legal standards for determining unfair electoral boundaries, such as the Eisen v. Constantine court case, in an effort to achieve a more objective definition of fairness. We believe that this method will contribute significantly to a fair electoral system in the United States. Due to space constraints, our discussion of the theoretical foundations of this technique has been omitted. We plan to elaborate on the theoretical aspects in future publications. Furthermore, the detailed numerical data used in our analysis has been excluded due to space constraints. We aim to make this data publicly available through arXiv in the future. Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual environment understanding in AI, as they synchronize a text-based narrative with in-game reality. Current AI models excel in processing text but struggle to integrate this into a game-like setting, leading to slow interactions (approximately 10 actions per second) that hinder large-scale training. We introduce TextWorldExpress, an optimized platform that bridges this gap by leveraging a specialized virtual machine, resulting in significant performance enhancements of up to 100-fold, enabling massive datasets of one million steps to be created. In addition, we showcase how our platform can be used to rapidly replicate and extend prominent text-based games like Zork and the Magic Engine. With the capability to exercise vast creativity, these expanded games can serve as a robust foundation for developing and testing cutting-edge AI models. The code and game definitions for TextWorldExpress are openly accessible on GitHub and GitHub. Moreover, a demo of the platform can be accessed via Repl.it. Further information about our research is available on our website. We utilize the approach of A-spectrum, recently introduced by Avila and Santos, to identify and characterize edge states in topological insulators with various types of defects. By applying this method to the Rashba and Dresselhaus models under different conditions, we find that it effectively detects spatially extended states associated with states at the bulk spectrum. Notably, the approach remains reliable even in the presence of disorder, such as random spin-dependent potentials, and can accurately determine the spatial localization of states. Furthermore, the size of systems required to characterize topological properties is significantly reduced, from a linear system size for existing methods to a polynomial size with respect to the number of atoms. Additionally, the approach allows for the efficient characterization of non-chiral topological properties. To validate our findings, we conduct numerical simulations using a fully numerical hybrid method that combines exact diagonalization and tight-binding representations. We find that this new approach provides a powerful tool for characterizing topological properties in systems with defects. As such, it has the potential to greatly advance the study of topological insulators, particularly those with various types of defects that may limit the use of other methods. We envision that this approach will be useful in experiments using small systems where special care must be taken to characterize the low-energy states. In particular, the reduced system size makes the approach more suitable for analyzing the properties of topological insulators in certain types of nanofabricated structures. Additionally, applying the approach to systems with a defect confined to a specific region allows us to conclude that edge states remain localized along curved surfaces, such as a circle, even in the absence of symmetry under spatial transformations. We find that the presence of Rashba and Dresselhaus terms contributes equally to the localization of states along these curved surfaces. Finally, we investigate the behavior of states fully extended in space when subjected to various types of disorder and find that an adequate system size is required to accurately characterize topological properties even in systems with disorder. Based on these findings, we propose a new method for determining the required system size based on the number of atoms in a system. The approach allows us to efficiently characterize non-chiral topological properties in systems with disorder and provides a new understanding of topological insulators with disorders. Additionally, we discover that in the presence of Rashba and Dresserhaus interactions, an adequate system size is required to characterize the properties of a system with a non-zero topological number. We find that the required system size scales polynomially with the number of atoms and provide a new formula

Assuming a growth condition, we establish a unique $p$-harmonic function within the sector $\Sigma$ that displays linear growth, and subsequently derive comparisons and estimates for $p$-harmonic functions within the sector. Furthermore, we define a Lusin $p$-harmonic function as the weak solution to a quasilinear elliptic equation and investigate its properties within the sector $\Sigma$. This allows for comparisons of extreme storm surge events to be analyzed in a spatial context. The key to our proof is our development of a novel theorem regarding the interaction between finite sums of products of specific value-corrected functions, one of which is highly irregular and the other draws from a base domain of algebraic numbers. By demonstrating that any non-constant polynomial can be broken down into a specific combination of these value-corrected functions, with specific constraints, we conclude our findings. Achieving successful human-to-human or human-to-Robot interactions in operability scenarios requires careful adaptation of tasks tailored to individual human partners, taking into account their unique operational habits. The challenges posed by differing human preferences for task execution, along with their inherent variability in pose and orientation, demand a flexible and adaptive approach. Such an approach must be able to modify a task's associated geometric structure in real-time, effectively "shaping" it to align with the corresponding human's operational framework. The proposed solution involves utilizing the Conditional Riemannian Normalization (CRN) algorithm to achieve this task adaptation, by mapping a task's features to a human's preferred operational framework using the Parallel Transport-CRN (P-CTRn) technique. A turntable is an effective tool in visual photography and scanning, but its application is limited when the object in question isn't designed for rotation. In contrast, this research demonstrates that almost any object can be an effective turntable if moved around in an irregular shape, thereby facilitating 3D shape reconstruction through observation. A simple, low-latency method is proposed to training a neural network, which effectively utilizes irregular paths to accurately determine an object's 3D position, thereby supporting downstream tasks including material editing, object manipulation, and shape reconstruction. The primary advantage of this method lies in its capacity for autonomous data collection, thereby eliminating the need for an initial 3D model scan. The observed results reveal that the turntable approach can consistently outperform state-of-the-art object reconstruction methods, even when trained on unorganized point cloud data. Furthermore, this technique exhibits robustness in the face of limited supervision, which makes it particularly suitable for real-world applications. The code for this project is openly accessible on GitHub. In addition to the proposed method, an open-source dataset containing over 50 million images of everyday objects in their natural settings is also being made available as a public resource. This dataset, denoted as the "Unintended Turntable Dataset" (UTD), can serve multiple purposes, such as training object detection models and supporting downstream tasks mentioned above. Ultimately, the primary intention behind this research is to promote more effective autonomous data collection techniques that don't rely on expensive equipment or complex algorithms. The demonstrated results reveal that 3D shape reconstruction can be achieved through observed irregular movements, which has far-reaching implications across multiple domains. The proposed method also highlights the significance of autonomous data collection in deep learning, which can potentially be extended to other areas beyond object reconstruction. In particular, this technique can be adapted to various applications including but not limited to autonomous driving and navigation in irregular terrain. In conclusion, the main contribution of this research lies in the deployment of a turntable as a means of achieving 3D shape reconstruction using observed irregular movements, which has led to the establishment of a large-scale open dataset containing over 50 million images. In addition to supporting 3D shape reconstruction, the same approach can also be used in material editing, object manipulation, and other related tasks. The code for this project, as well as the UTD dataset itself, are being made available as public resources. In particular, the UTD dataset can be utilized for training models that require 3D shape information, which encompasses a range of object-related tasks

Additionally, our model reveals the existence of a threshold for pulse generation and shows that increasing the strength of the IR field can generate shorter pulses, but only up to a certain point, beyond which the pulses disappear in a burst. We attribute this behavior to the electron ionization threshold and illustrate the importance of vacuum interaction for understanding APG mechanisms. Our calculations indicate that weaker, more damped pulses can still be generated if the IR field oscillations are not perfectly synchronized, and that reducing the electron initial velocity can produce shorter pulses in a specific time frame. After analyzing the data, they concluded that none of the reported companions in the recent surveys could be attributed to such a low-mass companion. This method creates new vertices in the grid based on the residual values at each node, adjusting the grid spacings accordingly to minimize error. We demonstrate that the capacity of these FeFETs significantly varies according to the domain configuration, resulting in a substantial increase in capacity that is contingent on the domain orientation. Due to its minimal resistance, this capacity can be the predominant factor in the devices' overall capacity. Consequently, in order to accurately model FeFETs, it is essential to capture this capature-voltage interaction and resulting current conduction enabled by the domain walls. We employ numerical simulations across diverse domain configurations and scenarios, such as domain wall motion induced by an applied voltage, to validate the simulation framework. The results of these simulations support the notion that the capature and corresponding current conduction enabled by the domain walls are crucial aspects that must not be overlooked. A specific condition on the jump mechanism is introduced, which essentially limits the size of jumps in relation to the frequency of occurrence. Under these conditions, sufficient criteria are established for irreducibility using a relatively simple approach, which relies on analyzing stochastic evolution equations with compact propagation domains. This paper examines the minimal degree of the power graph of finite nilpotent groups. The power graph of a group is defined as the set of elements resulting from raising other elements to various positive powers. We establish a degree estimate for the power graph of finite nilpotent groups based on their ranks. Additionally, we determine the power graphs of groups of rank two and three, then derive an estimate for the degree of such graphs. Notably, our result implies the existence of a group with a power graph of infinite degree. We also provide further examples and discuss an associated question. The proof of our degree estimate involves several complex concepts, including the Discrete Logarithm Problem, the Polya Enumeration Formula, and the transfer homomorphism. These tools yield approximate degree counts, but often yield exact degrees in the groups we examine. Conversely, some of our degree estimates remain precise, while others require further refinement. We employ both combinatorial and group-theoretic approaches to confirm our degree estimates. Ultimately, our power graph investigations seem to be novel in the literature, and so our methods and conclusions are likely analogous for other groups with similar characteristics. We hope our work will spur further research into power graphs and related problems. We pose an associated question: does every finite group have a power graph with bounded degree? We anticipate a negative response, and our work seems to be a step in that direction. We also discuss several related questions, and provide some further examples and observations. We establish that abelian groups have power graphs with degree at most four, and that non-abelian groups can only have a power graph with degree at most three if they are of rank two. We also examine some specific examples of groups with power graphs of degree three. We construct two groups with power graphs of degree two and three, respectively, and then demonstrate that many groups cannot have a power graph with degree two by examining associated polynomial equations. We establish that finite groups with a power graph of degree two must have rank at most three. We also examine some group-theoretic properties associated with the power graphs of finite groups, and then investigate an analogous problem for finite semigroups. We establish upper bounds for the degree of the power semigroup of finite groups and 3-groups, and then construct examples that nearly reach these bounds. We also examine some related questions for finite semigroups. Ultimately, our work seems to be a starting point for further research into power graphs and related problems. We anticipate a deeper understanding of these groups through further research into power graphs

Recently, neural network Trojan attacks have gained significant interest due to their potential to secretly manipulate model decisions without being detected. The traditional approach to these attacks involves training them within the host network's architecture, which has several limitations in terms of scalability and confidentiality. For example, the attack is tied to a specific host model and cannot be applied to other networks. Additionally, its purpose can be inferred from its trained structure. In this work, a new type of hostless Trojan attack is proposed that operates outside of host models and can be carried out using just the input data. This novel attack leverages semantic manipulation through the employment of two separate generators, one for Trojan feature generation and the other for modifying semantic information in the target model's input. For instance, in image classification tasks, the feature generator creates artificial semantic features that can trigger the backdoor activation, while the semantic generator modifies the input image to incorporate these features, hiding the attack's existence from the target model's developers. Successful activation of the backdoor is achieved by designing a semantic label in the input data for the target model, which triggers the backdoor activation. The goal of our research is to determine the chemical properties of stars that host planets with masses less than 10 Earth masses by analyzing their elemental abundance patterns. We used a detailed stellar model to accurately measure the chemical properties of these stars. Between 2010 and 2019, high-dispersion spectroscopy data were collected for 27 stars that host planets with the HARPS3.8 instrument on the Swiss 1.23-meter telescope at La Silla Observatory in Chile. We examined abundance patterns for 12 essential elements and explored the relationship between these elements, as well as other correlations. Our study revealed connections between chemical properties and the mass, size, and orbital characteristics of the planets hosted by these stars. Our investigation of abundance patterns among the stars reveals two distinct groups, with the elements these stars are deficient in, affecting planet formation. Through comparisons with solar abundance patterns and other data, we determined mass limits for the planets hosted by these stars. Our analysis of abundance patterns among the stars reveals what the interior of these planets are made of. Based on our analysis, we conclude that the majority of the planets hosted by these stars have compositions that are primarily rocky. Additionally, among the planets with masses less than 3 Earth masses, those with larger sizes are more likely to be composed primarily of rock, whereas those with smaller sizes may have water and other volatile substances in their composition. In contrast, planets with masses greater than 3 Earth masses exhibit a diverse range of compositions. Furthermore, among the planets hosted by these stars, those with shorter orbital periods and higher temperatures are more likely to be composed primarily of rock, whereas those with longer orbital periods and lower temperatures may have water and other volatile substances in their composition. In summary, our analysis demonstrates that the diversity in the chemical properties of these planets is closely linked to their mass, size, and orbital characteristics, resulting in a wide range of compositions, with the potential for these planets to be composed entirely of rock or water and other volatile substances. Moreover, our study highlights the significance of understanding abundance patterns among the stars in predicting the chemical properties of exoplanets. Finally, our analysis demonstrates that no relationships exist between the abundance patterns among the stars and those of the planets hosted by these stars. Instead, the abundance patterns among the stars are closely linked to the mass, size, and orbital characteristics of these planets. Our findings are consistent with observations of the super-Earths and Neptune-like planets having rocky or water-rich compositions, as well as those of the massive planets exceeding the mass of Neptune

Inspired by how the human brain processes information, we developed an attention-based DNN (A-DNN) to focus on the CSI data relevant to localization. In cubic bipartite graphs, a robustly injective edge tinting refers to a coloring of the edges using two colors such that any given edge is part of at most one monochromatic cycle. We have discovered a counterexample to a previous conjecture stating that cubic bipartite graphs always receive a robustly injective edge tinting. The counterexample we found specifically involves a particular class of infinite graphs where the conjecture's requirements are not met. This counterexample shows that in order to prove the conjecture, additional restrictions must be imposed on the graphs in question. The counterexample we found can be used to create an infinite number of distinct cubic bipartite graphs that do not receive a robustly injective edge tinting. By examining these graphs in detail, the minimum size of cycles that prevent a robustly injective edge tinting in bipartite cubic graphs was identified. Uncertainty in data is a common issue in scientific investigations that spans various fields such as signal processing, computer science, and statistics. This research focuses on uncertainty related to data labeling or analysis, particularly final data interpretation. We refer to this type of uncertainty as ambiguity. Following a detailed analysis of existing methods, we introduce a standardized framework for evaluating ambiguity quantification techniques. This framework consists of three layers: the first assesses the impact of ambiguity on results, the second explores potential solutions to mitigate ambiguity, and the third investigates ways to reduce ambiguity through data collection adjustment. A comprehensive study is conducted to compare various techniques across different fields. Notably, our work highlights the distinct goals and approaches of different research areas to address ambiguity. Ultimately, the choice of AQI depends on the specific research objective: utilizing a straightforward method on high-confidence data, while addressing ambiguity with more advanced techniques. This multidisciplinary study is the first to provide an in-depth review of various techniques to address different types of ambiguity and compare algorithms within a unified framework. It is now publicly available as an open-source resource for researchers and practitioners to inform their research and future work. As research on this topic is highly interdisciplinary, our work aims to promote cross-domain understanding and facilitate future contributions. We welcome readers to explore our published study in greater detail, published at arXiv:2207.11467. New research developments are welcomed on our dedicated webpage: https://ambigquant.github.io/. Additionally, we find compact quantum groups where this algebra is isomorphic to a direct product of two C*-algebras, one being M_n(|G|), while in another example, it is isomorphic to a direct product of three C*-algebras, one being M_n(|G|), revealing a key symmetry property. When dealing with large-scale Markov Decision Processes, the value function can be approximated by dividing it into regional subsets. However, the algorithm may become stuck in an infinite loop if the value function hasn't converged sufficiently. Building on previous research, we suggest modifying the Generalized Minimum Residual method to create an iterative solution for large-scale MDPs. We compare this new approach with existing techniques when working with real-world data from the fields of supply chain management and healthcare. The results show that the improved algorithm requires fewer iterations and less computational time to yield comparable results to more complex algorithms. Moreover, it can provide accurate solutions within set confidence intervals, thus enabling the user to determine when additional computations are justified. Hierarchy refinement is an optional feature that can improve performance by simplifying the problem by removing less significant decision-making elements. We validate the effectiveness of this improvement by simulating a variety of scenarios in which the complexity of the problem is varied. Ultimately, the research demonstrates that the algorithm can effectively tackle large-scale MDPs of different scales and complexity levels. The code for this research is open-source and available at https://github.com/jmariogz/HiGMRES. In this research, we aim to mitigate this limitation by proposing a method to explicate the implicit mapping between system models and time series data. To gauge a student model's level of knowledge, assessing its performance across various geographic areas can provide valuable insights, offering a diverse perspective on its capabilities. However, determining which locations to use for evaluation purposes involves several considerations, including balancing the level of difficulty and relevance to the target application. In the context of learning intelligent systems, gaining a deeper understanding of a student model's expertise in specific regional contexts can be beneficial. A situation arises where student models may exhibit variations in their performance based on geographical location due to differences in data availability, cultural specificity, and the complexity of the environment. As such, there is a need to develop effective evaluation methods that can harmonize and build on these regional perspectives worldwide. 

This research focuses on developing methods to make the most out of regional queries in the context of peer assessment. Specifically, we aim to address the following critical questions: Which types of knowledge domains benefit from regional assessment mechanisms? How can we optimize regional evaluation methods to yield more valuable insights? 

We propose the use of a global knowledge domain typology to explore the benefits and limitations of regional queries in various knowledge areas. To this end, we create a set of criteria to gauge the usefulness of regional evaluation methods, and apply these criteria to peer assessment scenarios to guide the development of student models. We also present an illustrative example of integrating regional evaluation methods into the training of intelligent student models. 

In the long run, this research aims to contribute to the establishment of common standards and best practices for the evaluation of intelligent student models. We hope that our work will spark interesting discussions and inspire further collaboration in the field of peer assessment.

High-energy particles called jets are studied in collisions between lead ions at the Large Hadron Collider to understand how heavy particles interact with the created quark-gluon plasma. Analyzing isolated photons linked with jets allows us to observe modifications to the jets' structure caused by interacting with the plasma. This study uses data from lead-lead collisions at a 5.02 TeV energy and compares the behavior of jets in these collisions to those in proton-proton collisions. By examining the relationship between the isolated photon's energy and the associated jet's structure, we found evidence of changes within the jets. These changes suggest that the formation of certain particles within the jets is reduced, indicating that the plasma's influence goes beyond the jets' initial formation. By comparing the star formation rates (SFRs) derived from different methods, we can gain insight into the potential biases of SFR estimation. In this study, we set up a benchmark test to evaluate SFR derivation by comparing it with constraints from the Brackett-$\gamma$ line. To do this, we developed a new line SFR calibration using 21-cm Hα observations and narrow-band imaging of the same 82 galaxies at 0.02 < z < 0.05. We found that line SFRs are 2.3 times higher than those estimated using SED fitting, which suggests a general underestimation of SFRs by SED fitting. In addition, we found that the SFR discrepancy depends on the SED fitting method used, with some techniques yielding up to 3.5 times higher line SFRs relative to SED fitting. We also explored the causes of the underestimation of SFRs by SED fitting and proposed two possible explanations: dense star formation and dust obscuration, which may lead to underestimating SFRs by a factor of 2-3 even in the presence of SED fitting. To further investigate these possibilities, we developed two new dust laws and demonstrated that dense star formation could account for an underestimation of SFRs by a factor of 1.5-2. Alternatively, we proposed that dust obscuration could lead to an underestimation of SFRs by a factor of 2 and an overestimation of dust mass by a factor of 3. By testing these scenarios, we were able to achieve a reasonable agreement between observed and predicted line SFRs in nearly all cases, which suggests that the underestimation of SFRs by SED fitting is primarily due to dense star formation rather than dust obscuration. Based on our findings, we estimated that dust obscuration accounts for an underestimation of SFRs by a factor of 1.25 and predicted even higher factors at higher redshifts. Furthermore, we found that the underestimation of SFRs by SED fitting is largely independent of the dust temperature profile used and suggested that future studies aim to sample a wide range of star formation rates, including those associated with very dense star formation. By doing so, we can deepen our understanding of the complex processes that affect SFR estimation and refine the calibration of line SFRs. This study presents an innovative approach to synthesizing speech of varied lengths using a median-based non-statistical method, rooted in Transformative Sample Space Framework. We demonstrate how this method can generate synthetic data by varying one feature at a time, holding the rest constant, and show that its mode corresponds to the median of the target distribution. We illustrate the method's applicability in speech synthesis via two illustrative examples, showcasing its ability to produce synthetic speech with predetermined durations. We also compare our approach with existing statistical methods in speech synthesis and find that it outperforms them in certain aspects. We believe that the method's generality will enable its adoption in a wide range of generative models. We have made the code available for public access at https://github.com/vaibhavvaidya/Median-Driven-Speech-Synthesis. We intend to explore the method's extension to multiple feature variations in future work. We propose calling the method "Median Sample Space Framework" (MSS) in future research. It is observed that the synthetic samples produced by our approach exhibit a room mean squared error of 0.19. We have established a relationship between the number of samples taken and the distribution convergence, noting that as the number of samples taken approaches infinity, the synthetic distribution converges to the target distribution. We have tested the method's robustness to the order of feature variation and found that it performs equally well regardless of the order. We have used the method to create synthetic speech lengths of varying durations, demonstrating its capability. We have tested the method's performance under various conditions and found it to be more sample-efficient than existing statistical methods in speech synthesis.
